question: Can vegetable oils and fried foods cause cataracts?
answer_short: Wallach blames heavy vegetable-oil intake with low selenium, plus heated or hydrogenated 'trans' oils, for the free-radical rancidity that damages the eye and drives cataracts.
claim_text: Wallach says heavy consumption of vegetable oils together with low selenium, plus heated or hydrogenated 'trans' oils, drives the free-radical rancidity of cellular fat behind cataracts.
verbatim: Selenium also functions to protect cellular and organelle bi-lipid layer membranes from oxidative damage. Highintakes of vegetable oils, including salad dressing and cooking oils, concurrent with a selenium deficiency is the quickest route to a cardiomyopathy heart attack, arteriosclerosis (build up of plaque in the arteries resulting from free radical damage to the “intima” or lining of the Posty cataracts, macular degeneration, dementias, eainiiple sclerosis, cancer, etc. The polyunsaturated configuration of oils when heated or treated with hydrogen (“trans fatty acids”) literally causes the rancidity (“free radical” damage) of cellular fat.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach says heavy consumption of vegetable oils together with low selenium, plus heated or hydrogenated 'trans' oils, drives the free-radical rancidity of cellular fat behind cataracts.

Selenium's job is to keep the fats in your cells from oxidizing; vegetable oils are polyunsaturated fats that oxidize easily — especially once heated or hydrogenated into trans fats. So Wallach's warning is about the combination: flood the body with rancidity-prone oils while selenium (the antioxidant that would protect them) runs low, and the oils go rancid inside your cells, driving free-radical damage. He calls high vegetable-oil intake concurrent with selenium deficiency “the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer,” and ties the same pairing — including too much fish oil — to birth defects, arteriosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, and sudden cardiac death. The practical point: to him these oils aren't just empty calories, they actively consume the protection selenium is meant to provide.

Wallach warns that a diet high in vegetable oils (salad dressing, cooking oils) combined with low selenium is the fastest path to heart attack and cancer, because heating or hydrogenating the polyunsaturated oils turns them into trans fats and rancid, "free radical"-damaged cellular fat.

Hydrogenation and trans fats — Wallach's warning. Commercial food-makers pump hydrogen gas into liquid vegetable oils ('hydrogenation') to harden them into margarine, creating trans fatty acids. Wallach's stance: hydrogenated and partially-hydrogenated oils, once sold by the medical trade as a safe butter substitute to PREVENT hardening of the arteries (arteriosclerosis), fatty-plaque buildup (atherosclerosis) and stroke, are now known to be a DIRECT CAUSE of those very diseases. Fried foods, super-heated carbohydrates (breads, French fries, croutons), margarines, cooking oils and trans fats produce the inflammation that damages the arterial lining (intima), leading to clogged and blocked arteries, blood clots, thrombosis and stroke.

Wallach considers cancer to be, at root, a selenium-deficiency disease. Selenium is the body's most efficient antioxidant (the active mineral in the glutathione peroxidase enzyme system) and, per the review he cites, "a versatile anticarcinogenic agent." When selenium runs low, the immune system becomes depressed and cells lose their protection: body fats peroxidize (free-radical damage), carcinogens go undetoxified, and cellular respiration falls (his cited rule of thumb: "more oxygen less cancer"), allowing the malignant transformation of cells. He states that cancer "appears to be the result of a depressed immune system that has run out of essential nutrients, including selenium," and further associates it with carcinogen contact and high vegetable-oil intake.

Wallach teaches that age spots (liver spots) are rancid fat — ceroid lipofuscin or trans fatty acids — from cell walls accumulating under the skin; ten on the back of the hand mean millions in the organs, and they flag a high risk of cancer and heart disease. Because they are reversible, his treatment is to eliminate all fried foods and vegetable oils (salad dressing, cooking oils, margarine) plus sugar, with selenium and vitamin E.

To Wallach, fibromyalgia isn't an unexplained chronic-pain condition but a nutritional muscle disease under a modern name — the same thing veterinarians call white muscle disease or stiff lamb disease, and what he terms adult-onset muscular dystrophy. He notes it was eliminated from lambs, calves, and pigs back in 1957 through nutrition. In humans he frames it as a multiple-deficiency disease with a dietary trigger: a high intake of fried foods and vegetable oils (margarine, cooking oils) combined with deficiencies of selenium, vitamin E, and the sulfur-bearing amino acids. The logic mirrors his selenium thesis throughout — rancidity-prone oils flooding in while the antioxidants that would protect the muscle are missing — so his answer to the pain is to correct the deficiencies and cut the oils, not to mask symptoms with muscle relaxants.

Wallach says fibromyalgia -- the aching, weak-muscle cousin of chronic fatigue -- is a multiple-deficiency disease caused by a high intake of fried foods and vegetable oils together with shortfalls of selenium, vitamin E and the sulfur amino acids, and he treats it by eliminating the oils and supplementing selenium, vitamin E, essential fatty acids and an amino-acid program.

question: What kind of fat is in chocolate?
answer_short: Cacao butter is stearic acid (34%), palmitic acid (20%) and oleic acid (30%) - the oleic acid being the same mono-unsaturated fat found in olive oil.
claim_text: Wallach gives the fat composition of cacao butter, the fat in chocolate, as stearic acid (34%), palmitic acid (20%) and oleic acid (30%); stearic and palmitic are saturated fats, while oleic acid is a mono-unsaturated fat also found in olive oil.
verbatim: Cacao butter, the fat in chocolate, is comprised of stearic acid (34%), palmitic acid (20%) and oleic acid (30%). Both stearic and palmitic acids are saturated fats; oleic acid is a mono-saturated fat that is also found in olive oil.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach identifies oleic acid as a monounsaturated fat -- the same type of fat found in olive oil. He points to it as a major component of cocoa butter, the fat in chocolate: cocoa butter is roughly 34 percent stearic acid, 20 percent palmitic acid, and 30 percent oleic acid. Stearic and palmitic acids are the saturated fats in that mix, while oleic acid is the monounsaturated portion, the fraction he links to olive oil.

Wallach cites a Harvard School of Public Health review of 136 studies which concluded that chocolate is a major source of flavonoids (epicatechins, catechins and procyanidins) and that its primary fat, stearic acid, does not have adverse effects on blood vessels, cholesterol or overall cardiovascular health because it is metabolized differently than other saturated fats.

Who should take digestive aids, and why. Wallach gives this instruction as part of preventing candidiasis — the Candida albicans overgrowth he ties to chronic fatigue syndrome — and the reasoning is what makes the advice land. Candida is a normally harmless yeast living on the skin, mouth, vagina and intestine. It turns pathological when the gut's competing normal bacteria are killed off by long-term antibiotic use, or when low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, usually the result of salt restriction) lets it move up into the stomach — a location it does not normally occupy. Stress reduces stomach acid once it reaches the point of decompensation, and food allergies change the lining of the gut in a way very similar to celiac disease, raising the nutrient concentration in the gut into a 'hyperfertilized' environment the yeast finds attractive; eventually the overgrowth spills into the bloodstream. So his prevention starts with knowing your own digestive and absorptive patterns: pulse-test for food allergies, avoid long-term antibiotics, and as you grow older take betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal decrease in stomach-acid production. He is emphatic on two more points — take these digestive aids if you are under stress, and deal aggressively with any disease that lowers your immune capacity.

Wallach breaks with the idea that acne is just a teenage hormone or hygiene problem: he calls it primarily the result of an essential fatty acid deficiency, made worse by eating too much saturated and damaged polyunsaturated fat — the kind in fried foods and margarine. His fix is to cut the fast food, supply the missing good fats (essential fatty acids at about 3% of daily calories, or 9 grams a day), and check for food allergies, rather than reaching first for antibiotics.

Wallach describes calcium as essential to all living organisms and the fifth most abundant mineral in the earth's crust and biosphere. It is also the most abundant mineral in the human body: about 99 percent of it forms the hydroxyapatite crystal that gives bones and teeth their structure, while the remaining one percent works as a cofactor and activator — regulating the electrochemical functions of cells, releasing energy from ATP (adenosine triphosphate) for muscle contraction, driving blood clotting, triggering neurotransmitter release, and helping regulate the heartbeat. He argues that humans are biochemically designed for high-calcium diets, that modern American diets are critically deficient in it, and that supplementation is the only practical way to get enough.

In Wallach's chart of the classic essential amino acids, valine's function is listed as protein production—it is one of the amino acids the body strings together as a raw building block to make its proteins. Valine shares this straightforward 'protein production' role with lysine, threonine, leucine, and isoleucine, while other essentials in the same chart play more specialized parts: tryptophan as a precursor of niacin and serotonin, phenylalanine of thyroxin and epinephrine, methionine in forming choline and creatine phosphate, and histidine in forming histamine.

Wallach frames fibromyalgia as a multiple-deficiency disease (the same 'white muscle disease' eliminated in livestock in 1957) and treats it by eliminating vegetable oils and fried foods while supplementing EFAs at 9 grams/day, selenium at 300 mcg/day, vitamin E at 1,200 IU/day, and sulfur amino acids (methionine, cysteine, cystine).

question: Are vegetarians and vegans at higher risk of weak bones?
answer_short: Wallach warns they can be -- because of high phytic-acid intake, vegetarians and vegans who don't supplement 'always' develop mineral deficiencies, including bone-building calcium and copper.
claim_text: Wallach warns that vegetarians and vegans who don't supplement always develop mineral deficiencies -- including bone-building calcium and copper -- because of their high phytic-acid intake.
verbatim: Vegetarians and vegans who do not supplement with minerals rarely have P deficiency, however, because of their high phytic acid intake they always have other mineral deficiencies including Ca, Cu, Cr, V. Li and Zn.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach observes that vegetarians and vegans who do not supplement with minerals rarely have a phosphorus deficiency — unless they have chronic gluten intolerance from heavy whole-grain consumption. However, because of their high phytic-acid intake from raw vegetables, they always have other mineral deficiencies, such as calcium, copper, chromium, vanadium, lithium and zinc, unless they supplement.

Because phosphorus is part of most proteins, Wallach warns that high-protein diets raise phosphorus intake, which increases the body's calcium requirement and can aggravate osteoporosis, arthritis, high blood pressure, and loose teeth. Phosphorus also occurs as phytates in cereal and grain flours, so bread made from unleavened flour lets phytic acid bind calcium, iron, zinc, and other minerals and lower their absorption.

Wallach considers estrogen the wrong treatment for osteoporosis, and a risky one: it may be contraindicated because of a carcinogenic effect — it is known to cause breast and uterine cancer. His deeper objection is that he does not see osteoporosis as an estrogen-deficiency disease at all, but as a mineral-and-absorption failure — his program corrects stomach acid with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes and supplies calcium, magnesium and the plant-derived colloidal minerals (including boron) that bone actually needs. In that view hormone replacement treats a symptom while missing the real deficiency.

Strontium is a trace mineral most highly concentrated in mammalian bone. Wallach says it can replace calcium in many organisms, including man, and that there is considerable evidence it is essential in mammals. He associates a strontium deficiency with certain calcium- and boron-resistant forms of osteoporosis and arthritis.
Wallach says obesity is a serious predisposing factor to high blood pressure, and that losing weight can drop elevated blood pressure dramatically.

For aching spinal joints Wallach's joint-pain program adds cartilage, unsweetened gelatin, copper, manganese, sulfur, B6 and calcium-magnesium, plus chiropractic for the spinal, rib and pelvic subluxations.

Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body, with about 99% in the bones and teeth (as hydroxyapatite) and the rest used as a cofactor for blood clotting, muscle contraction, and the heart's electrical conduction. Wallach states that, contrary to the medical belief that high calcium causes kidney stones, a high dietary calcium intake actually reduces the risk of nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcemia, and kidney stones, and that no fewer than 147 deficiency diseases are attributed to calcium deficiency or imbalance. His Common Calcium-Deficiency Diseases include: osteoporosis (with kyphosis, scoliosis, Dowager's hump, lordosis, spontaneous fractures), receding gums, osteomalacia, myelosclerosis, arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, bone spurs, kidney stones, nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, hypertension, insomnia, calcium deposits (vascular, restless leg, atrial fibrillation), cramps and twitches (Tourette's syndrome), premenstrual syndrome, low-back pain (sciatica), neuropathy (Bell's palsy, trigeminal neuralgia), tetany with convulsions, and panic attacks. In his words: 'There are no less than 147 different deficiency-diseases that are directly attributed to a calcium deficiency or imbalance.'

Sodium is one of the three indispensable electrolytes (with chloride and potassium); it makes up about two percent of the body's mineral content and, with chloride, is mainly extracellular. Together these electrolytes maintain normal water balance and distribution, osmotic equilibrium, acid-base balance, and muscular and nerve excitability, all under adrenal-cortex and pituitary hormonal control. Wallach explains that 'salt hunger' is one of the most basic cravings of animals and man, strongest in herbivores and human vegetarians because grains, vegetables and fruit contain little sodium chloride. Addison's disease (failure of the adrenal cortex) causes a loss of sodium and potassium retention with general weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss and a marked salt hunger, relieved by salt supplementation. Sodium-chloride deficiency arises mainly in hot weather or heavy exercise with profuse sweating; Wallach warns that 'water intoxication' killed infants fed low-sodium formulas -- their brains swelled from a simple sodium deficiency -- and that the treatment for sodium deficiency is water and salt, taken orally or as 0.9% intravenous saline.

question: Can a copper deficiency make hair dry and brittle?
answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists dry, brittle hair (the 'steely wool' seen in copper-deficient sheep), along with white, gray and silver hair, among the signs of copper deficiency.
claim_text: Among the diseases and symptoms of copper deficiency, Wallach lists white, gray, and silver hair and dry brittle hair — the “steely wool” seen in copper-deficient sheep.
verbatim: Diseases and Symptoms of Copper Deficiency White hair, gray hair, silver hair Dry brittle hair (“steely wool” in sheep)

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach classifies hemorrhoids as varicose veins, the rectal-and-anal form of the same weakened vessel walls (which he attributes to copper deficiency) that also produce leg varicose veins, spider veins, and aneurysms.

Wallach prints a long table of the conditions he attributes to copper deficiency — many tied to copper's role in pigment, connective tissue and blood vessels. Hair and skin: white/grey/'silver' hair, vitiligo (loss of skin pigment), dry brittle hair. Sagging and weakened tissue: ptosis (drooping eyelids, 'crow's feet,' sagging skin/breasts/belly), hernias, varicose veins, hemorrhoids, spider veins, and aneurysms (rupture-prone weak spots in artery walls) — including Kawasaki disease (congenital aneurysms with streptococcal infections). Also anemia, hypo- and hyperthyroid dysfunction, arthritis, disc disease and liver cirrhosis. Neuro-behavioral: violent behavior / blind rage / 'criminal' behavior, learning disabilities (ADD, ADHD, some autism), cerebral palsy, and aplasia/hypoplasia (underdevelopment) of the cerebellum. Copper-deficiency brain diseases across species: enzootic ataxia in sheep, Mad Cow Disease in cattle, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans. Plus elevated blood cholesterol (above 350), iron storage disease (hemosiderosis), reduced carbohydrate tolerance, and neutropenia (low neutrophil count). In his words: "Copper deficiency Symptoms and Diseases: White, grey and 'silver' hair; Vitiligo; Dry brittle hair; Ptosis; Hernias; Varicose veins (including hemorrhoids); Spider veins; Aneurysms; Kawasaki disease; Anemia; Hypo and hyperthyroid dysfunction; Arthritis; Disc disease; Liver cirrhosis; Violent behavior, blind rage, explosive outbursts and 'criminal' behavior; Learning disabilities (ADD, ADHD, some forms of autism); Cerebral palsy, aplasia and hypoplasia of the cerebellum; Enzootic ataxia in sheep; Mad Cow Disease in cattle; Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease; Elevated blood cholesterol (above 350); Iron storage disease (hemosiderosis); Reduced carbohydrate tolerance; Neutropenia."

Premature gray, white, or silver hair is, in Wallach's reading, the first visible sign of copper deficiency — because copper is the cofactor the body needs to manufacture hair pigment. He backs it with a favorite story: a flock of turkeys dying of ruptured aortic aneurysms whose deaths stopped once copper was doubled in the feed, since copper also builds the strong elastic fibers in artery walls. Other copper-shortage signs he lists include skin wrinkles, spider and varicose veins, and an iron-resistant anemia.

Copper is a universally important cofactor for hundreds of metalloenzymes -- required for the pigment melanin (hair and skin color), for lysyl oxidase that gives blood vessels, skin, and discs their tensile strength, and for oxygen handling in respiration; Wallach calls copper deficiency widespread and notes it underlies several diseases the medical community wrongly blames on prions or infection. Copper-deficiency diseases include: white/gray/silver and dry brittle hair, ptosis (sagging eyelids, skin, breasts, belly), hernias, varicose and spider veins (hemorrhoids), aneurysms, Kawasaki disease, Marfan's syndrome, anemia, hypo- and hyperthyroid, arthritis, ruptured and bulging discs, liver cirrhosis, violent/blind-rage/explosive/criminal behavior, learning disabilities, cerebral palsy with cerebellar hypoplasia (congenital ataxia), high cholesterol, iron-storage disease, reduced glucose tolerance (hypoglycemia, reactive hypoglycemia), and neutropenia.

Wallach lists copper-deficiency signs that appear in many forms, including: white, gray and dry brittle hair; ptosis (sagging tissue of eyelids, skin, breasts, stomach); congenital and acquired hernias; varicose veins; aneurysms (including cerebral artery blowouts); Kawasaki disease (congenital aneurysms with streptococcal infection); anemia (especially on vegan and high-milk diets); hypo- and hyperthyroid; arthritis; ruptured vertebral disc; and liver cirrhosis.

Wallach explains that hair pigment is a type of melanin formed by the enzyme tyrosinase acting on the amino acid tyrosine, and that copper is required as the cofactor for this reaction. When copper is deficient, pigment production fails and the hair turns white, silver or gray.

Tyrosine is the starting material the body uses to make melanin, the pigment that colors hair and skin. The enzyme tyrosinase acts on tyrosine to build the pigment, and this reaction requires copper as a cofactor. Wallach points out the practical consequence: when copper is deficient, the reaction stalls and hair turns white, silver, or gray. He also notes that red hair is a different case -- its pigment (tricosiverin) is an iron-based compound rather than ordinary melanin.

Wallach catalogs a broad set of zinc-deficiency signs and diseases: loss of the sense of smell and taste, infertility, failure of wounds and ulcers to heal, immune failure, poor growth and short stature, high infant mortality, hypogonadism, anemia, and hair loss (alopecia). He also lists pica or cribbing — abnormal cravings to eat things like dirt, wool, or hair. In his framework these are not separate mysterious illnesses but the visible fingerprint of one missing mineral.

question: Do whole grains and a high-protein diet block the minerals my gums need?
answer_short: Wallach says yes — a high-protein diet plus the phytates in cereals and whole-grain flours bind calcium, iron and zinc and lower their absorption, which can loosen teeth and worsen periodontal disease.
claim_text: Wallach warns that a high-protein diet and the phytates in cereals and whole-grain flours bind up calcium, iron, zinc and other minerals and lower their absorption, which can loosen teeth and drive periodontal disease.
verbatim: Phosphorus is part of most proteins and as such becomes problematic because elevated P intake increases Ca requirements when “high protein diets” are consumed. Under those circumstances P can aggravate osteoporosis, arthritis, high blood pressure, loosen teeth, periodontal disease, etc. Phosphorus is present as phytates in cereals and whole grain flours, therefore, if bread is made from unleavened flours, the phytic acid will complex with Ca, Fe, Zn, and other minerals further lowering their absorption rate.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Because phosphorus is part of most proteins, Wallach warns that high-protein diets raise phosphorus intake, which increases the body's calcium requirement and can aggravate osteoporosis, arthritis, high blood pressure, and loose teeth. Phosphorus also occurs as phytates in cereal and grain flours, so bread made from unleavened flour lets phytic acid bind calcium, iron, zinc, and other minerals and lower their absorption.

Wallach explains that phosphorus is present as phytates in cereals and whole grain flours. When bread is made from unleavened flours, the phytic acid complexes with calcium, iron, zinc and other minerals in the gut, further lowering their absorption rate. This is why phosphorus in grain form can work against the very minerals the body needs.

How well calcium is absorbed depends heavily on its form and the gut environment. It is taken up mainly in the duodenum while the contents are still acidic; once the intestine turns alkaline, absorption falls off. Plain metallic calcium may be only 1-3% absorbed, whereas an organically bound, plant-derived colloidal or water-soluble chelated form can reach up to 98%. Wallach lists the causes of a calcium deficiency as: too little vitamin D; low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, which can follow a salt-restricted diet); lactose intolerance; celiac disease; a high-fat or low-protein diet; and heavy fiber and phytate intake. Phytic acid (in grain bran, oatmeal, whole wheat) and oxalic acid (in rhubarb, spinach, chard, mustard greens) each bind calcium into insoluble, unabsorbable salts, and excess sugar, carbonation and caffeine leach stored calcium from the bones.

Wallach explains that phytates are phytic acid — chemically inositol hexaphosphate — found abundantly in whole grains and raw vegetables, and that this same compound interferes with the absorption of calcium, iron, zinc and other nutrients, making it a required nutrient on one hand and a dietary negative on the other.

Wallach identifies salt (sodium chloride) as the raw material the stomach needs to manufacture its acid, so people on salt-restricted diets are more prone to achlorhydria (loss of stomach acid). Achlorhydria brings 'burp, belch, and bloat,' lets intestinal bacteria and yeast ferment high-carbohydrate foods in the stomach, and leads to B12, calcium, and protein deficiencies plus new adult-onset food allergies from absorbing partly digested proteins -- so his treatment starts with putting salt back on your food.

According to Wallach, causes of calcium deficiency include a lack of vitamin D and a deficiency of stomach acid — the low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria) itself often stemming from a salt-restricted diet. Lactose intolerance, celiac disease, high-fat diets, low protein intake, and high phytate consumption also lead to deficiency. In the same discussion he notes phytic acid in grain bran binds calcium into unabsorbable calcium phytate, oxalic acid in foods like spinach and rhubarb forms unabsorbable calcium oxalate, and dietary fiber itself prevents calcium absorption.

Iron is an essential mineral; a healthy adult carries 3 to 5 grams, most of it in hemoglobin and myoglobin, where iron carries oxygen (iron is to hemoglobin what magnesium is to chlorophyll). Wallach stresses that pica -- obsessive cravings driving children and adults to eat ice (pagophagia), dirt (geophagia), lead-paint chips and high-calorie snack foods -- is a specific sign of iron deficiency, and that the snack-food form can cause weight gain and obesity. Iron deficiency arises from unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation, chronic infection, hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid from salt-restricted diets or proton-pump inhibitors), chronic diarrhea, chronic bleeding, and impaired absorption from high-fat or high-phytate diets and gluten intolerance. Its symptoms include listlessness, fatigue, heart palpitations on exertion, rapid pulse (tachycardia), reduced cognition and memory, sore tongue, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and hypochromic microcytic anemia. Stomach hydrochloric acid and vitamin C aid absorption; heme iron from meat is 10 percent absorbable versus 1 percent from plants (phytates bind it). He notes excess iron storage can be caused by deficiencies of selenium, copper or zinc and is falsely blamed for liver cirrhosis, pancreatic fibrosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes.

Wallach observes that vegetarians and vegans who do not supplement with minerals rarely have a phosphorus deficiency — unless they have chronic gluten intolerance from heavy whole-grain consumption. However, because of their high phytic-acid intake from raw vegetables, they always have other mineral deficiencies, such as calcium, copper, chromium, vanadium, lithium and zinc, unless they supplement.

question: Can eating too much white rice cause nerve damage?
answer_short: Wallach says yes -- beriberi, a nervous-system disease of weakness, numbness and paralysis, is caused by the loss of thiamine (vitamin B1) when the bran is polished off white rice.
claim_text: Wallach explains that beriberi -- a nervous-system disease of weakness, numbness and paralysis -- is caused by the loss of thiamine (vitamin B1) when the bran is polished off white rice.
verbatim: In 1901, Dr. Gerrit Grijns, a Dutch doctor, has shown that Beri- beri, a disease that affects the nervous system and is characterized by weakness, numbness, and paralysis is caused by the deficiency of a nutrient (thiamine - B1) removed when white rice is polished (re- moval of the bran).

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Beriberi is the classic thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency disease. Wallach describes it as a common disease of the Asian rice cultures (the name is Sinhalese for 'I cannot'), characterized by weakness in the legs, hands, and arms together with congestive heart failure, with death from pulmonary edema and abdominal 'dropsy.' He identifies the cause as a thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency — historically appearing where the diet was polished white rice with its thiamine-bearing bran removed.

According to Wallach, mild vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency produces mental confusion, muscular weakness, peripheral paralysis, calf muscle tenderness, muscle fatigue, emotional instability, loss of appetite, loss of interest in daily tasks and general lethargy. Chronic deficiency advances to a polyneuritis and congestive heart failure with edema and life-threatening pulmonary edema. The signs therefore span both the nervous system and the cardiovascular system.

Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a cofactor for energy production and the metabolism of carbohydrates, protein, and fat; its deficiency especially disturbs carbohydrate metabolism in the brain (dementia) and heart (congestive heart failure). Wallach lists the health problems of thiamine deficiency: anxiety, hysteria, confusion, nausea, depression, mental confusion, loss of appetite (anorexia), muscular weakness, fibromyalgia, beriberi (muscle wasting, congestive heart failure, Korsakoff syndrome with dementia, and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome with dementia and multiple sclerosis), paralysis, and peripheral neuropathies. In his words: 'Thiamine (B,)-deficiency health problems include: Anxiety, hysteria, confusion; Nausea; Depression; Mental confusion.'

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive disease of the central nervous system marked by scattered zones of demyelination (loss of the fatty insulating layer on nerves). Symptoms start between ages 20 and 40 — usually tingling or numbness in the arms or legs (a 'stocking and glove' pattern) — and progress to weakness, clumsiness, visual and balance problems, dizziness and bladder-control trouble; intention tremor, nystagmus and 'scanning' speech form Charcot's triad. Wallach links MS to mercury (he cross-references mercury poisoning) and to the loss of cholesterol-rich myelin. He criticizes the orthodox cortisone/prednisone approach and instead recommends: avoid animal fats; a high intake of fish oil (cod liver or salmon oil) at 5 grams three times a day and flaxseed oil at one tablespoon twice a day (said to raise survival by 50 percent); removal of mercury (amalgam) fillings; calcium 2-aminoethylphosphate (CaEAP) one dose four times a day; octacosanol two capsules three times a day; daily snake-venom injections; D-phenylalanine at 500 milligrams three times a day; betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day; avoidance of known food allergens with rotation diets; and avoiding vitamin C supplements (using green vegetables and juices as a natural source instead). Wallach says the same regimen has also worked for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, or Lou Gehrig's disease).

Wallach's vitamin table lays out what a thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency does, and it reaches from the heart to the mind. The classic form is beriberi, which can bring on congestive heart failure, but he stresses the neurological toll too: memory loss (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome), mental confusion, depression, lethargy, muscular weakness and even paralysis, emotional instability, and loss of appetite. It underlies his repeated point that 'senility' and heart failure can have a simple vitamin cause.

Wallach recounts the naval evidence that beriberi is a dietary deficiency disease. The Japanese ship Riuyo returned from an extended voyage in 1883 with 25 dead sailors and 144 others stricken with beriberi. In 1884 naval surgeon Kanekiro Takaki joined an identical voyage and proved that a diet built primarily on polished rice was the cause; by changing the diet to include sources of thiamine (vitamin B1), the disease could be prevented and cured.

The very word 'vitamin' traces back to thiamine (vitamin B1). Wallach explains that Funk produced a crystalline substance from rice polishings and yeast that could prevent and cure experimentally produced beriberi. Because the substance was a basic (high-pH) nitrogen compound — an amine essential to life — Funk called it a 'vit- (vital) amine.' The term was then accepted as a broad label for dietary substances deemed to be dietary essentials.

Wallach lists the signs of thiamine (vitamin B-1) deficiency: anorexia (loss of appetite), brain atrophy (senility), confusion, constipation, coordination impairment, depression, dyspnea (labored breathing), gastrointestinal upset, edema, fatigue, irritability, memory loss, muscle atrophy, nervousness, numbness of the hands and feet, pain hypersensitivity, palpitations, sonophobia (sound sensitivity), and weakness.

question: What really causes obesity in children?
answer_short: Wallach says childhood obesity comes from mineral-deficiency pica, not TV, video games, or lack of outdoor play, and that giving kids more minerals would reverse it.
claim_text: Wallach blames childhood obesity on mineral-deficiency pica rather than on television, video games, or a lack of outdoor play, saying mineral-starved children who cannot eat dirt instead consume more soft drinks, juice, and junk food.
verbatim: Dickens and Ford reported that twenty five percent of children eat dirt. We believe that mineral deficiency pica occurs in American children at a much higher rate than twenty five percent; we believe it occurs at eighty to 100 percent, however, because of the social con- straints against eating dirt, kids will instead consume more soft drinks, more juice, more French fries, more cookies, more cake, more pasta and generally more calories as a result of their mineral deficiencies. This mineral deficiency driven pica, not playing outdoors, watch- ing TV and playing video games, is the cause of obesity in kids.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach defines pica — cribbing and cravings for things like dirt, paint, snack food, sugar, and salt — as a symptom of one or more nutritional mineral deficiencies, insisting that only mineral deficiencies cause this behavior. In adults it shows up as cravings for ice, chips, salsa, chocolate, and soft drinks; in children as eating dirt or paint chips. His remedy is mineral supplementation, including plant-derived colloidal minerals, rather than willpower.

Wallach rejects the genetic, lack-of-exercise, and overeating explanations for obesity and identifies it instead as a mineral-deficiency disease: the body's unmet mineral hunger manifests behaviorally as food cravings, binge eating, the 'munchies,' and pica (the eating of non-food items). The remedy is correcting the underlying mineral deficiency rather than relying on gastric bypass, calorie restriction, or willpower. He notes he and Ma first reviewed obesity in Rare Earths: Forbidden Cures (1994) and published their definitive findings in Hell's Kitchen (2006). In Hell's Kitchen, Wallach argues that a deficiency of two or more essential minerals produces significant pica, cravings and binge eating. Wallach explains pica and 'cribbing' — the compulsion to eat non-food items — as a sign of zinc deficiency. Rather than treating these cravings as purely psychological, he reads them as the body signaling a mineral shortfall, one that also shows up in unsupplemented athletes who lose heavy zinc in sweat.

His treatment includes religious use of hypoallergenic baseline nutritional supplements (no corn, wheat, soy, egg, or milk); avoiding vaccinations of egg, blood, or beef origin; vitamin C to bowel tolerance; vitamin A at 300,000 international units a day as beta carotene; bioflavonoids at 150-300 milligrams a day; zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day; essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times a day; selenium at 200 micrograms three times a day; chromium at 50-200 micrograms three times a day; betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-500 milligrams three times a day before meals; adrenal cortical extract; autoimmune urine therapy; five-day rotation diets; and avoidance of offending foods (intestinal repair takes up to 90 days, and intravenous hydrogen peroxide speeds healing).

Night terrors (nightmares) are almost always caused by food allergies and hypoglycemia. Wallach uses the pulse test and a six-hour glucose tolerance test to find the cause, noting blood sugar bottoms out about 4 to 4.5 hours after eating (especially sugary foods), so night terrors tend to strike roughly four hours after a bedtime snack such as cookies and milk. Bedwetting in children often accompanies night terrors and likewise stems from food allergies (usually milk) and hypoglycemia. Treatment: avoid offending food allergens and sugar, chromium at 25-200 micrograms three times a day, a high-animal-protein diet, the baseline nutritional supplement program, and avoid caffeine.

Obesity (overweight) is, at its simplest, consuming and storing more calories than you use — but Wallach stresses it is not simple. Starvation backfires (the body conserves energy), so eat at least 1,000 calories a day for gradual, permanent loss, with moderate exercise (walking, tennis, golf, swimming, low-impact aerobics). He says 90 percent of obese people overeat and binge because empty-calorie diets trigger 'pica' — a nibbling driven by the body's search for trace minerals — so use colloidal minerals. Test for food allergies (pulse test) and do a six-hour glucose tolerance test for hypoglycemia or diabetes. His program: avoid food allergens, sugar (solid and liquid), caffeine and carbonated drinks (phosphates promote osteoporosis); drink filtered spring water, 8-10 glasses a day; use potassium salt with kelp; don't skip meals (large breakfast, moderate lunch with animal protein, light soup-and-salad dinner); salmon oil at 5 grams three times a day, flaxseed oil one tablespoon twice a day, two tablespoons of nutritional fiber before bed, glucomannan at 1 gram before meals, betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day before meals, and thyroid starting at 1-3 grains (adjust to avoid jitteriness; needing over six grains suggests celiac-type malabsorption). Herbal laxatives or diuretic teas and subliminal weight-loss tapes can also help.

Wallach treats memory loss as an umbrella covering senile dementia, Korsakoff's syndrome, and Alzheimer's, and stresses it has a variety of causes rather than one -- so each possible cause should be looked up separately, including food allergies and hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). He recommends a pulse test to find food sensitivities and a six-hour glucose tolerance test (GTT) to confirm or rule out hypoglycemia. His treatment: avoid the offending food allergens plus sugar, fried food, margarine, and alcohol; then supplement chromium and vanadium at 25-200 mcg three times a day, selenium at 200-1,000 mcg a day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU a day, and B-complex at 50 mg three times a day. He adds the memory agents Diapid (vasopressin nasal spray) at 12-16 units a day, Lucidril (centrophenoxine) at 4.4-8.0 gm a day, Dinagen (piracetam) at 1.6-4.8 gm a day taken with choline, and hydergine at 9-20 mg a day. In Wallach's words: "MEMORY LOSS (senile dementia, Korsakoff's syndrome, Alzheimer's) can be much more devastating than a physical disability. There are a variety of causes of memory loss and it is suggested that you look up each one separately including food allergies and hypoglycemia."

Wallach argues that food allergies drive emotional problems like depression indirectly — the celiac-type gut damage they cause blocks absorption of the essential nutrients the body and nervous system need.

question: Does chocolate raise cholesterol?
answer_short: Studies Wallach cites say chocolate doesn't raise cholesterol or LDL and that cacao flavonoids boost blood flow to the heart, brain, hands and legs.
claim_text: Wallach cites studies reporting that chocolate does not raise cholesterol or increase LDL (Journal of the American College of Nutrition) and that the flavonoids in cacao can help increase blood flow to the heart, brain, hands and legs (Hypertension, 2003).
verbatim: Studies published in the Journal of the American College of Nutrition, reported that chocolate does not raise cholesterol or increase LDL. In a 2003 issue of the journal, Hypertension, it was reported that the flavanoids in cacao could help increase blood flow to the heart, brain, hands and legs.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach cites a Harvard School of Public Health review of 136 studies which concluded that chocolate is a major source of flavonoids (epicatechins, catechins and procyanidins) and that its primary fat, stearic acid, does not have adverse effects on blood vessels, cholesterol or overall cardiovascular health because it is metabolized differently than other saturated fats.

Wallach uses Japan as a counterexample to the anti-salt orthodoxy. He notes that while American doctors told patients to eat less than one gram of salt per day, the Japanese by contrast consumed about fifteen grams of salt per day. Despite this, he reports, the Japanese had eighty-five percent less cardiovascular disease and hypertension than Americans — evidence he uses to argue that high salt intake is not the cause of heart disease or high blood pressure.

Vanadium is a trace mineral Wallach credits with several cardiovascular actions. One he calls the 'inotropic effect' — vanadium increases the contractile force of the heart muscle, making each beat stronger. In the same passage he reports that it also inhibits cholesterol synthesis (lowering both blood and aortic cholesterol) and shows anticarcinogenic properties in animal studies, where it blocked induced mammary tumors in mice. Vanadium is best known in his framework as chromium's partner against adult-onset diabetes.

Essential fatty acids matter most where growth is fastest, and Wallach flags their deficiency in infants specifically: it results in poor growth, eczema, and lowered resistance to infectious disease. He frames these good fats as far more than fuel — they lower serum cholesterol and are the raw material for prostaglandins, the local hormones that help regulate blood pressure, heart rate, blood-vessel and airway width, clotting, and brain and spinal-cord function.

Wallach considers cholesterol above 270 mg per 100 ml of blood a rising risk for heart disease, diabetes and liver disease, but cautions that a level driven below 200 can be equally or more dangerous than a high one.

Wallach states it is well documented that flavonoids play a positive role in reducing cardiovascular disease risk. They inhibit coagulation, thrombus formation, and platelet aggregation, reduce the risk of atherosclerosis, and lower arterial blood pressure and hypertension. They also reduce oxidative stress in vascular cells, modify vascular inflammation, improve endothelial and capillary function, adjust blood lipid levels, help regulate carbohydrate and glucose metabolism, and even modify the mechanisms of aging.

Essential fatty acids (EFA) are the fats the body cannot make for itself and so must get from the diet. Wallach names three polyunsaturated ones - linoleic, linolenic and arachidonic acid - and notes only two (linoleic and linolenic) are strictly essential, since the body can build arachidonic acid from linolenic; 3% of daily calories must come from EFAs. They do vitamin-like jobs: carrying and processing fat, keeping cell membranes intact, lowering blood cholesterol, and serving as the raw material for prostaglandins that help regulate blood pressure, heart rate, blood-vessel and airway width, blood clotting, and brain and spinal-cord function. A shortage is especially damaging in infants.

Vitamin B12 (and its cobalt) does some of the body's most fundamental work. Together with folic acid, choline and the amino acid methionine, it transfers single-carbon (methyl) groups used to build RNA and to make DNA from RNA — so it sits at the heart of gene function, which is why Wallach ties preconception nutrition to preventing birth defects. Growth, the formation of myelin (the insulating sheath — made by converting cholesterol — around nerves in the brain, spinal cord and large nerve trunks), and red-blood-cell production all depend on B12. Cobalt is also a required cofactor for making the thyroid hormone thyroxine.

question: What foods help prevent cataracts?
answer_short: Wallach points to antioxidant-rich foods -- berries, red grapes, pomegranate, broccoli, kale, spinach, red bell peppers and green tea -- to fight the free radicals behind cataracts.
claim_text: Wallach names antioxidant-rich foods -- berries, red grapes, pomegranate, broccoli, kale, spinach, red bell peppers and green tea -- as protection against the free radicals behind cataracts.
verbatim: Antioxidants are found in substantial quantities in: Fruit - blueberries, cherries, kiwis, pink grapefruit, oranges, plums, prunes, raisins, raspberries, red grapes, strawberries, boysenberries, pomegranate, noni and mangostein. Vegetables - alfalfa, beets, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, eggplant, kale, tomatoes, red bell peppers, spinach, tomatoes. Green tea - EGCG Antioxidants are essential to a long and healthy life and they are especially important to the obese human and the obese per- son who wants to loose weight. When body fat is burned, waste products (trans fats, oxidized fats and ceroid lipofucsin) are pro- duced. These fat metabolism waste products are free radicals and they significantly increase the risk of cancer, heart disease, vascular disease (arteriosclerosis, atherosclerosis), thrombotic disease (stroke, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and coronary thrombosis), macular degeneration, cataracts and Alzheimer’s disease.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach says daily antioxidant-rich food and drink quench the free radicals that raise cataract risk, and puts the optimal intake at 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points a day.

Antioxidants are the body's defense against free radicals — the reactive molecules that oxidize and damage your cells, cell walls and mitochondria. Wallach's signature point is that they don't work alone: the antioxidant enzyme systems present in every healthy cell need raw materials and mineral cofactors to run at full capacity — glutathione, for example, requires selenium. So in his framework, getting the benefit of antioxidants is inseparable from getting the minerals that power them, and he measures the antioxidant strength of foods by their ORAC score.

ORAC stands for Oxygen Radical Absorbance Capacity, a lab score for how strongly a food, drink or supplement neutralises free radicals. The test scores one specific attacker, the peroxyl radical, chosen because it is among the most common reactive oxygen species in the human body. Worth noting that Wallach's books print the name two ways - Absorbance in Immortality, Absorption in Hell's Kitchen.

Dr. Wallach lists noni among the fruits that contain antioxidants in substantial quantities, alongside blueberries, cherries, kiwis, pink grapefruit, oranges, plums, prunes, raisins, raspberries, red grapes, strawberries, boysenberries, pomegranate and mangosteen. He believes antioxidants will be added to the list of essential nutrients, because without them the body cannot protect itself from dietary and environmental free radicals or attain maximum life spans. He stresses this especially for people burning body fat, since burned fat produces free-radical waste products (trans fats, oxidized fats and ceroid lipofuscin).

Wallach's daily target is 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points, which he gives as the optimal intake for reaching the age of 100. It is a maintenance figure, not a cure, and he never presents it alone: in the same book he pairs it with cutting free-radical foods such as fried food, trans fats, burnt fat, nitrites, alcohol and sugar, taking every essential nutrient with a special focus on minerals, and a calorie-restricted diet. He is also explicit that antioxidants by themselves raise a population's average lifespan but not its maximum.

Wallach's method for reversing the aging pigment has three parts: cut free-radical foods hard, take every known essential nutrient, and push antioxidants to 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points a day. The foods he names to cut are fried foods, trans fats, burnt fats, heterocyclic amines, super-heated carbohydrates, acrylamides, nitrites, alcohol and sugar. He frames the whole thing inside Clive McKay's equation - a calorie-restricted diet without malnutrition yielding a 30 to 100 percent longevity increase - where without malnutrition means every known essential nutrient at optimal levels well above the RDI, with a special focus on minerals.

In the ORAC table of common foods and drinks that Dr. Wallach reproduces in Immortality, noni juice is listed with an ORAC (Oxygen Radical Absorbance Capacity) value of 398 per serving, near the other exotic juices he cites (mangosteen juice at 498 and wolfberry/goji juice at 363). Wallach uses ORAC as the measure of a food's antioxidant / free-radical-neutralizing power, and states that the optimal total daily intake to reach the age of 100 is 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points per day.

Wallach considers cancer to be, at root, a selenium-deficiency disease. Selenium is the body's most efficient antioxidant (the active mineral in the glutathione peroxidase enzyme system) and, per the review he cites, "a versatile anticarcinogenic agent." When selenium runs low, the immune system becomes depressed and cells lose their protection: body fats peroxidize (free-radical damage), carcinogens go undetoxified, and cellular respiration falls (his cited rule of thumb: "more oxygen less cancer"), allowing the malignant transformation of cells. He states that cancer "appears to be the result of a depressed immune system that has run out of essential nutrients, including selenium," and further associates it with carcinogen contact and high vegetable-oil intake.

question: Can a hair analysis reveal a hidden food allergy?
answer_short: When a hair test shows every mineral low, Wallach reads it as malabsorption -- frequently from an undetected wheat or cow's-milk allergy injuring the gut.
claim_text: Wallach says a hair analysis showing all minerals uniformly low points to malabsorption -- often from a hidden wheat gluten or cow's milk allergy damaging the gut.
verbatim: If all of the mineral levels in the hair analysis are universally low it indicates maldigestion ( hypochlorhydria - low stomach acid) and/or malabsorption ( celiac disease - wheat gluten or cows milk albumen allergy).

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach says even a good diet fails if you cannot absorb minerals, so he advises a pulse test to find food allergies that cause celiac-type gut changes and malabsorption, plus a hair analysis to check your mineral status.

Dermatitis (atopic dermatitis, eczema, and dermatitis herpetiformis) is a common skin disease that Wallach says is treated incorrectly with cortisone or prednisone creams; 97% of these patients have wheat-gluten food allergies and almost as many are sensitive to cow's milk, with the same lesions occurring in the small-intestine lining and causing serious, life-threatening, immune-depleting malabsorption (a precursor to diabetes, cancer, arthritis, and birth defects). His treatment for all three forms is a gluten-free and cow's-milk-free diet, a pulse test on frequently eaten foods, essential fatty acids at 5 gm four times daily, para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) at 200 mg four times daily, betaine HCl and digestive enzymes at 75-200 mg each three times daily before meals, vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, zinc at 50 mg three times daily, and colloidal minerals on top of the base-line supplement program; healing the intestinal lesions takes 60-90 days.

Pica (craving dirt or paint) is a symptom of one or more nutritional deficiencies: adults often crave ice, while children eat dirt and/or paint — the latter extremely dangerous because many paints contain lead or cadmium. A hair analysis is invaluable for assessing the patient's mineral status, and a pulse test helps determine whether a celiac-type malabsorption problem exists. Treatment should include the baseline nutritional program with plant-derived colloidal minerals; EDTA chelation therapy may be necessary if a hair analysis shows elevated levels of lead or cadmium.

Wallach cautions that hair-mineral readings need interpretation: universally low levels indicate maldigestion (hypochlorhydria) and/or malabsorption (celiac disease); and paradoxically "elevated" calcium and magnesium can mean active depletion/shedding from bone — revealing very active osteoporosis with associated arthritis, periodontitis and a predilection for kidney stones — while elevated sodium/potassium/chloride signal essential-fatty-acid deficiency.

Wallach ties poor appetite to mineral status, not just psychology: deficiencies of the minerals zinc and lithium are associated with anorexia (loss of appetite). In the same discussion he goes further, arguing that anorexia nervosa — usually treated as a psychiatric disease — is often a manifestation of a severe food allergy, since sufferers commonly feel better when they don't eat. His answer is to correct the deficiency, hunt down the offending food (frequently cow's milk, wheat, eggs, or corn), and support digestion with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes alongside the baseline vitamin-mineral program.

Wallach traces anxiety and panic attacks to one of two root causes -- a hidden food allergy (such as corn or cow's milk) or a sharp reactive-hypoglycemic blood-sugar crash -- with concurrent PMS often making it worse.
Wallach supplements eczema (atopic dermatitis) with essential fatty acids as flaxseed oil at 9 grams per day, plus vitamin E, taking the fats as intravenous interlipids if malabsorption is severe.

Diabetes, Wallach says, is easy to prevent, cure, and treat (avoiding blindness, hypertension, amputations, early death) — and since 1958 supplemental chromium has been known to prevent and treat both diabetes and hypoglycemia, with vanadium able to replace insulin for adult-onset diabetics. Diagnosis is easy: a six-hour glucose tolerance test shows blood glucose rising steeply (over 275 mg/dL at 30-60 minutes, possibly over 350 and staying elevated) with positive urine sugar. His treatment is chromium and vanadium at 25 mcg per day initially to prevent insulin shock, titrating up to 25 mcg twice then three times daily, then 50 mcg twice daily as insulin is reduced; betaine HCl and digestive enzymes at 75-200 mg three times daily before meals for the celiac-type intestinal lesions from food allergies (wheat gluten, cow's milk, soya); zinc at 50 mg three times daily; B-complex at 50 mg three times daily (including niacin, part of the glucose tolerance factor); essential fatty acids at 5 gm three times daily; vitamin B-12 at 1,000 mcg per day; bioflavonoids including quercetin at 150 mg per day; copper at 2-3 mg per day; lecithin at 2,500 mg three times daily; and glutathione at 100 mg per day, on a high-fiber diet with no processed carbohydrates. Useful herbs include licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra), jaborandi (Pilocarpus jaborandi), yarrow (Achillea millefolium), horseweed (Erigeron canadensis), and Jerusalem artichoke.

question: Can a thyroid or iodine deficiency be linked to varicose veins?
answer_short: In his African clinic Wallach saw iodine and copper deficiency together produce varicose veins, aneurysms, anemia, miscarriages, and goiter in adults.
claim_text: From his clinic work in Africa, Wallach reports that iodine and copper deficiency together produced anemia, varicose veins, aneurysms, miscarriages, and goiter in adults.
verbatim: Calcium deficiency caused osteomalacia in children and arthritis, and osteoporosis and kidney stones in adults. lodine and copper deficiency produced anemia, varicose veins, aneurysms, miscarriages, and goiter in adults.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: From his clinic work in Africa, Wallach reports that iodine and copper deficiency together produced anemia, varicose veins, aneurysms, miscarriages, and goiter in adults.

Premature gray, white, or silver hair is, in Wallach's reading, the first visible sign of copper deficiency — because copper is the cofactor the body needs to manufacture hair pigment. He backs it with a favorite story: a flock of turkeys dying of ruptured aortic aneurysms whose deaths stopped once copper was doubled in the feed, since copper also builds the strong elastic fibers in artery walls. Other copper-shortage signs he lists include skin wrinkles, spider and varicose veins, and an iron-resistant anemia.

Wallach classifies hemorrhoids as varicose veins, the rectal-and-anal form of the same weakened vessel walls (which he attributes to copper deficiency) that also produce leg varicose veins, spider veins, and aneurysms.

Copper is a universally important cofactor for hundreds of metalloenzymes -- required for the pigment melanin (hair and skin color), for lysyl oxidase that gives blood vessels, skin, and discs their tensile strength, and for oxygen handling in respiration; Wallach calls copper deficiency widespread and notes it underlies several diseases the medical community wrongly blames on prions or infection. Copper-deficiency diseases include: white/gray/silver and dry brittle hair, ptosis (sagging eyelids, skin, breasts, belly), hernias, varicose and spider veins (hemorrhoids), aneurysms, Kawasaki disease, Marfan's syndrome, anemia, hypo- and hyperthyroid, arthritis, ruptured and bulging discs, liver cirrhosis, violent/blind-rage/explosive/criminal behavior, learning disabilities, cerebral palsy with cerebellar hypoplasia (congenital ataxia), high cholesterol, iron-storage disease, reduced glucose tolerance (hypoglycemia, reactive hypoglycemia), and neutropenia.

Wallach frames goiter (an enlarged, or 'colloid,' thyroid) as a straightforward nutritional-deficiency disease rather than a mysterious gland disorder. It is caused by a simple deficiency of the nutrients the thyroid needs — chiefly iodine, but also copper, molybdenum, and the amino acid tyrosine. Goiter can also be driven by 'goitrogens' — substances such as the nitrates in luncheon meats, hot dogs, and fertilizer-contaminated well water, plus vegetables like cabbage, broccoli, and Brussels sprouts — which depress thyroid activity and can produce a goiter even when iodine is present in the diet. Starved of its nutrients, the thyroid gland swells 50 to 100 times its normal size, creating the visible lump at the front of the neck.

Wallach prints a long table of the conditions he attributes to copper deficiency — many tied to copper's role in pigment, connective tissue and blood vessels. Hair and skin: white/grey/'silver' hair, vitiligo (loss of skin pigment), dry brittle hair. Sagging and weakened tissue: ptosis (drooping eyelids, 'crow's feet,' sagging skin/breasts/belly), hernias, varicose veins, hemorrhoids, spider veins, and aneurysms (rupture-prone weak spots in artery walls) — including Kawasaki disease (congenital aneurysms with streptococcal infections). Also anemia, hypo- and hyperthyroid dysfunction, arthritis, disc disease and liver cirrhosis. Neuro-behavioral: violent behavior / blind rage / 'criminal' behavior, learning disabilities (ADD, ADHD, some autism), cerebral palsy, and aplasia/hypoplasia (underdevelopment) of the cerebellum. Copper-deficiency brain diseases across species: enzootic ataxia in sheep, Mad Cow Disease in cattle, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans. Plus elevated blood cholesterol (above 350), iron storage disease (hemosiderosis), reduced carbohydrate tolerance, and neutropenia (low neutrophil count). In his words: "Copper deficiency Symptoms and Diseases: White, grey and 'silver' hair; Vitiligo; Dry brittle hair; Ptosis; Hernias; Varicose veins (including hemorrhoids); Spider veins; Aneurysms; Kawasaki disease; Anemia; Hypo and hyperthyroid dysfunction; Arthritis; Disc disease; Liver cirrhosis; Violent behavior, blind rage, explosive outbursts and 'criminal' behavior; Learning disabilities (ADD, ADHD, some forms of autism); Cerebral palsy, aplasia and hypoplasia of the cerebellum; Enzootic ataxia in sheep; Mad Cow Disease in cattle; Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease; Elevated blood cholesterol (above 350); Iron storage disease (hemosiderosis); Reduced carbohydrate tolerance; Neutropenia."

Wallach lists copper-deficiency signs that appear in many forms, including: white, gray and dry brittle hair; ptosis (sagging tissue of eyelids, skin, breasts, stomach); congenital and acquired hernias; varicose veins; aneurysms (including cerebral artery blowouts); Kawasaki disease (congenital aneurysms with streptococcal infection); anemia (especially on vegan and high-milk diets); hypo- and hyperthyroid; arthritis; ruptured vertebral disc; and liver cirrhosis.

Wallach places iron storage disease and iron-resistant anemia among the symptoms of copper deficiency, alongside signs such as crow's feet, skin wrinkles, spider and varicose veins, hemorrhoids, and liver cirrhosis. In his framework these iron-labeled problems are actually signs of a copper shortage, not of iron itself.

question: Do trans fats raise your cholesterol?
answer_short: Yes — Wallach cites that trans fats raise LDL and triglycerides while lowering protective HDL cholesterol.
claim_text: Wallach cites nutrition professor Bruce Holub that trans fats, found in hydrogenated oils, raise LDL 'bad' cholesterol and triglycerides while lowering protective HDL 'good' cholesterol.
verbatim: “Besides increasing the number of LDL (bad) cholesterol and trig- lycerides in the bloodstream, trans fats also lower your HDL (good) cholesterol,” says Bruce Holub, Ph.D., a professor of nutrition at the University of Guelph, Canada. “Trans fats also increase blood levels of acompound called lipoprotein a. The more of this lipoprotein you have in your system, the greater your risk of developing heart dis- ease,” he said.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Selenium's job is to keep the fats in your cells from oxidizing; vegetable oils are polyunsaturated fats that oxidize easily — especially once heated or hydrogenated into trans fats. So Wallach's warning is about the combination: flood the body with rancidity-prone oils while selenium (the antioxidant that would protect them) runs low, and the oils go rancid inside your cells, driving free-radical damage. He calls high vegetable-oil intake concurrent with selenium deficiency “the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer,” and ties the same pairing — including too much fish oil — to birth defects, arteriosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, and sudden cardiac death. The practical point: to him these oils aren't just empty calories, they actively consume the protection selenium is meant to provide.

Wallach warns that a diet high in vegetable oils (salad dressing, cooking oils) combined with low selenium is the fastest path to heart attack and cancer, because heating or hydrogenating the polyunsaturated oils turns them into trans fats and rancid, "free radical"-damaged cellular fat.

To Wallach, fibromyalgia isn't an unexplained chronic-pain condition but a nutritional muscle disease under a modern name — the same thing veterinarians call white muscle disease or stiff lamb disease, and what he terms adult-onset muscular dystrophy. He notes it was eliminated from lambs, calves, and pigs back in 1957 through nutrition. In humans he frames it as a multiple-deficiency disease with a dietary trigger: a high intake of fried foods and vegetable oils (margarine, cooking oils) combined with deficiencies of selenium, vitamin E, and the sulfur-bearing amino acids. The logic mirrors his selenium thesis throughout — rancidity-prone oils flooding in while the antioxidants that would protect the muscle are missing — so his answer to the pain is to correct the deficiencies and cut the oils, not to mask symptoms with muscle relaxants.

Wallach argues there is clear evidence humans are designed to consume high-calcium diets, pointing to the late Paleolithic (35,000 to 10,000 years ago) as the last time humans lived in the environment they were biochemically designed for. The agricultural revolution 10,000 years ago narrowed the variety of wild foods while raising calorie intake, permanently lowering dietary minerals, trace minerals, and rare earths. Wild plants and game would have supplied Stone Age humans roughly 1,600 mg of calcium at rest and 2,000–3,000 mg at working energy levels, whereas 20th-century American adults take in only one-fifth to one-third as much — a median of 300–508 mg a day for women and just 680 mg for men.

Wallach's fourth dementia: Alzheimer's disease, which he calls a 'physician-caused' disease -- produced by lowering the patient's dietary cholesterol and saturated fat, prescribing statin drugs, and directing patients to avoid vitamin and mineral supplements. His prevention/treatment protocol is the same anti-dementia regimen used for the other three dementias: no fried foods, no processed meats, no oils; 4-6 eggs per hundred pounds of body weight per day; avoidance of all statin drugs (he cites an April 2012 FDA warning that statin drugs increase the risk of dementia and type 2 diabetes); and DHA and EPA essential fatty acids (omega-3) to support production of the neurotransmitters of memory and cognition. He cites a Johns Hopkins randomized double-blind ten-year study, published in 2004 on nearly 5,000 people over age 65, showing that a special diet plus nutrient supplementation can reduce Alzheimer's risk by 78%. In Wallach's words: "Prevention of Alzheimer's has been documented by a Johns Hopkins randomized and double blind study on almost 5,000 people over the age of 65. The ten-year study published in 2004 demonstrated clearly that the consumption of a special diet, avoidance of certain foods and the supplementation of nutrients can reduce the risk of Alzheimer's disease by 78%!"

Surprisingly, Wallach classifies aluminum as an essential nutrient - specifically the organically-bound colloidal aluminum found in all soil-grown plants, which he considers nontoxic. Its biological job: activating the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase. In animal studies, an aluminum-deficient diet produced congenital limb defects (non-genetic birth defects) in the young and liver cirrhosis (scarring) in adults, while supplementing it raised newborn survival - leading chemistry professor Gerhard Schrauzer to call it 'probably an essential mineral for human nutrition.'

Wallach points to boron's bone-protective and hormonal effects. He says it is needed both to maintain bone density and to keep normal blood levels of estrogen and testosterone. He cites a supplementation finding: within eight days of taking boron, women held on to far more of their minerals - excreting 40% less calcium, 33% less magnesium, and less phosphorus in their urine - while their level of 17-beta estradiol (the main, most active form of estrogen) doubled to what is seen in women on estrogen-replacement therapy, and testosterone doubled in both men and women.

Hydrogenation and trans fats — Wallach's warning. Commercial food-makers pump hydrogen gas into liquid vegetable oils ('hydrogenation') to harden them into margarine, creating trans fatty acids. Wallach's stance: hydrogenated and partially-hydrogenated oils, once sold by the medical trade as a safe butter substitute to PREVENT hardening of the arteries (arteriosclerosis), fatty-plaque buildup (atherosclerosis) and stroke, are now known to be a DIRECT CAUSE of those very diseases. Fried foods, super-heated carbohydrates (breads, French fries, croutons), margarines, cooking oils and trans fats produce the inflammation that damages the arterial lining (intima), leading to clogged and blocked arteries, blood clots, thrombosis and stroke.

question: Does cobalt play a role in the thyroid?
answer_short: Yes -- Wallach says cobalt is a necessary cofactor for making thyroid hormone, so it is another mineral the thyroid depends on besides iodine.
claim_text: Wallach says cobalt is a necessary cofactor the body needs to produce thyroid hormone.
verbatim: Cobalt is also a necessary cofactor for the production of thyroid hormone.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Iodine is an essential mineral concentrated in the thyroid gland; combined with the amino acid tyrosine it is manufactured into the thyroid hormone thyroxin, which regulates digestion, heart rate, body temperature, sweat-gland activity, the nervous and reproductive systems, general metabolism and body weight. Wallach argues iodine intake is usually low to begin with, and that as Americans restrict their salt intake on medical advice, physician-caused goiter and hypothyroidism have become epidemic; copper is a required cofactor for using iodine, so copper-poor soils also drive goiter. Low iodine and thyroid function produce hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's disease) -- fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hair loss, depression, constipation, dry skin, poor memory, goiter, infertility, and congenital birth defects (cretinism in the newborn). He notes many foods act as goitrogens that interfere with thyroid function (dietary and waterborne nitrates, cruciferous vegetables, gluten intolerance) and that about 11 million Americans have an under- or over-active thyroid; the average American takes in only 170 to 250 micrograms of iodine per day, and metallic iodine is not toxic up to 2,000 micrograms per day.

In Wallach's framework, cobalt is an essential trace mineral required by every form of life, from blue-green algae, bacteria and fungi to plants, insects and all the vertebrates including humans. It works as a cofactor and activator for enzymes and helps "fix" nitrogen during amino-acid production, but its defining role is nutritional: a single cobalt atom sits at the very center of vitamin B12 (the cobamide coenzymes). Because of that, the body's cobalt requirement is really a requirement for the finished B12 molecule — cobalt/B12 is needed to build DNA and RNA, form red blood cells, make the myelin that insulates nerves, and produce the thyroid hormone thyroxine. Cobalt is a rare element, making up only about 0.003% of the earth's crust, and where soils are cobalt-depleted the crops, animals and people that depend on them fall deficient.

The thyroid is Wallach's main reason for calling tyrosine essential. In combination with the mineral iodine, tyrosine is the amino acid the body manufactures into the thyroid hormone thyroxin, which governs metabolism. In his words: "all long lived peoples on earth eat red meat (including pork, beef, goat, lamb, etc.), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy"

Wallach is firmly against going vegan and puts chicken squarely inside a healthy, long-life diet. His core claim: every long-lived population on earth eats animal foods — red meat (pork, beef, goat, lamb), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy — and no vegan, he says, has ever lived to 100 or raised a thriving colony of healthy kids on the diet. Unsupplemented strict vegans, he warns, tend to develop grey hair, receding gums, osteoporosis, anemia, arthritis and even cancer within 5 years, and he points to vegan crusader Linda McCartney, who died at 56 of breast cancer.
Wallach recommends vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta-carotene for dermatitis and eczema, while the gut heals over 60-90 days.

Food allergies (sensitivities) are a concern for everyone, because the celiac-disease-type changes they cause in the intestines prevent absorption of essential nutrients; Wallach says anyone with a chronic disease (cancer, diabetes, arthritis, heart disease) and/or emotional problems (hypoglycemia, depression, neurosis, schizophrenia, hyperactivity, paranoia) has food allergies, identifiable by the Coca pulse test and a diet diary. His treatment includes religious use of hypoallergenic baseline nutritional supplements (no corn, wheat, soy, egg, or milk); avoiding vaccinations of egg, blood, or beef origin; vitamin C to bowel tolerance; vitamin A at 300,000 international units a day as beta carotene; bioflavonoids at 150-300 milligrams a day; zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day; essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times a day; selenium at 200 micrograms three times a day; chromium at 50-200 micrograms three times a day; betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-500 milligrams three times a day before meals; adrenal cortical extract; autoimmune urine therapy; five-day rotation diets; and avoidance of offending foods (intestinal repair takes up to 90 days, and intravenous hydrogen peroxide speeds healing).

Periodontal disease (receding gums, pyorrhea, gingivitis) is blamed by 'orthodox' dentists on food particles packing between the teeth and gums, but Wallach says all forms are really the result of bone loss under the gums, which lets the gums recede — and he points out the veterinary profession eliminated it through nutrition (cows, horses, dogs, and cats do not floss, brush, or use fluoride mouthwash). Treatment should correct the dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio (give up phosphate-containing soft drinks, reduce red meat, reduce phytate intake from raw vegetables), supplement calcium at 2,000 milligrams and magnesium at 1,000 milligrams per day, follow the baseline nutritional supplement program with plant-derived colloidal minerals, vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day, betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day fifteen minutes before meals, avoid sugar, and use herbal and hydrogen-peroxide mouthwashes plus dental floss to keep the teeth clean.

Wallach describes how much of routine obstetric and gynecologic self-care can be done at home. A woman can perform her own monthly breast self-examination, take advantage of free or reduced-fee mammograms, do a self internal (vaginal and cervical) examination, and track her cycles so any abnormal change is noticed immediately. Pregnancy can be diagnosed at home with over-the-counter home pregnancy test kits, and prenatal vitamins are sold without a prescription — he urges any sexually active woman to be on a baseline vitamin-and-mineral supplement program to prevent birth defects. He notes a woman can weigh herself, take her own blood pressure and test her own urine, send blood to the public-health lab for Rh, anemia and toxoplasmosis testing, take a LaMaze class to understand labor, and request a hospital or university ultrasound to locate the placenta, confirm the baby's age and rule out twins. Except for twins, placenta previa, pelvic deformity or Rh problems, he says a woman can have her baby at home.

Wallach counts zinc among the foundational essential minerals — a nutrient the body cannot make and has to be supplied daily. The adult body holds only about 1.4 to 2.3 grams of it, stored mainly in the liver, pancreas, kidney, bone, and muscle, yet that small amount does outsized work: no fewer than 70 metalloenzymes — including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, and carboxypeptidase — require zinc as a cofactor before they can work at all. Zinc is also built into the RNA molecule (the 'zinc fingers') and is needed for cell division, DNA synthesis, growth, immunity, wound healing, taste and smell, and healthy skin, hair, and nails. Because it touches so many systems, Wallach ties a long list of deficiency signs and birth defects to a shortage of it, and he includes zinc as a daily essential in his Base Line supplement program.

Korsakoff's syndrome is a form of recent-memory loss that Wallach calls a "false Alzheimer's disease": the person can still perform detailed tasks they learned before the illness began, but can no longer record or store new memories or learn even the simplest new task. A telltale feature is confabulation — inventing imaginary experiences to fill in for memories that can't be recalled. Wallach traces it to a single vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, usually caused by chronic alcoholism combined with a diet heavy in sugar and simple carbohydrates; it can also follow a blow to the head. Because it is a thiamine deficiency and not true Alzheimer's, he considers it reversible — patients are routinely misdiagnosed with Alzheimer's yet can be cured within a week once given megadoses of thiamine. His treatment centers on high-dose vitamin B1 (100 mg three times a day) along with lecithin, strict avoidance of alcohol and sugar, chromium and vanadium, betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes, and other memory-supporting agents. When alcohol has actually damaged the brain tissue, the alcoholic form is called Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and is harder to treat.

To Wallach, fibromyalgia isn't an unexplained chronic-pain condition but a nutritional muscle disease under a modern name — the same thing veterinarians call white muscle disease or stiff lamb disease, and what he terms adult-onset muscular dystrophy. He notes it was eliminated from lambs, calves, and pigs back in 1957 through nutrition. In humans he frames it as a multiple-deficiency disease with a dietary trigger: a high intake of fried foods and vegetable oils (margarine, cooking oils) combined with deficiencies of selenium, vitamin E, and the sulfur-bearing amino acids. The logic mirrors his selenium thesis throughout — rancidity-prone oils flooding in while the antioxidants that would protect the muscle are missing — so his answer to the pain is to correct the deficiencies and cut the oils, not to mask symptoms with muscle relaxants.

Hydrogen is an essential structural element: it is the major constituent of water (about 70 percent of the human body is water) and of all organic molecules, and Wallach frames the body's acid-base balance as, in fact, the regulation of hydrogen-ion (H+) levels in cellular and extracellular fluids. He notes a practical corollary: bladder infections (cystitis) can often be controlled by acidifying the urine with unsweetened cranberry juice.
