tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach frames gluten intolerance not as an allergy but as a 'contact enteritis' -- an irritant reaction of the small-grain proteins on the gut lining, analogous to the contact dermatitis poison ivy causes on skin (no one is allergic to poison ivy, yet nearly everyone is intolerant of it). The gastrointestinal damage from this gluten-contact enteritis includes celiac disease, diverticulitis, appendicitis, irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel syndrome, leaky gut syndrome, colitis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, gastritis, bloating, and reflux. The gradual, progressive loss of intestinal villi it causes produces malabsorption and, through it, a wide range of nutritional-deficiency diseases -- so the corrective action is to avoid gluten. In his words: 'The gastrointestinal damage that is produced by the gluten-contact enteritis includes celiac disease (wheat allergy that occurs concurrently with contact enteritis), diverticulitis, appendicitis, irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel syndrome, leaky gut syndrome, colitis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, gastritis, bloating, and reflux.'

Folic acid (folate, vitamin B9) is required for the synthesis of DNA, RNA, and red blood cells and works interdependently with vitamin B12; a deficiency of either produces a megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia. Wallach notes the deficiency arises from a diet lacking green leafy vegetables and from malabsorption (gluten intolerance, celiac disease, leaky gut syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome), and lists its health problems: impaired cell division, birth defects (neural tube defects such as spina bifida), failure to thrive, anemia, diarrhea, bleeding gums, weight loss, and irritability. In his words: 'The deficiency of folic can result from a diet lacking in green leafy vegetables and from malabsorption problems (such as gluten intolerance [includes bourbon, scotch and beer], celiac disease, leaky gut syndrome, IBS, etc.)'

Iodine is an essential mineral concentrated in the thyroid gland; combined with the amino acid tyrosine it is manufactured into the thyroid hormone thyroxin, which regulates digestion, heart rate, body temperature, sweat-gland activity, the nervous and reproductive systems, general metabolism and body weight. Wallach argues iodine intake is usually low to begin with, and that as Americans restrict their salt intake on medical advice, physician-caused goiter and hypothyroidism have become epidemic; copper is a required cofactor for using iodine, so copper-poor soils also drive goiter. Low iodine and thyroid function produce hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's disease) -- fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hair loss, depression, constipation, dry skin, poor memory, goiter, infertility, and congenital birth defects (cretinism in the newborn). He notes many foods act as goitrogens that interfere with thyroid function (dietary and waterborne nitrates, cruciferous vegetables, gluten intolerance) and that about 11 million Americans have an under- or over-active thyroid; the average American takes in only 170 to 250 micrograms of iodine per day, and metallic iodine is not toxic up to 2,000 micrograms per day.

Many medications interfere with folic acid absorption and metabolism, according to Wallach, including methotrexate, aspirin, oral contraceptives, anti-convulsives, anti-psoriatic drugs, and cancer treatment pharmaceuticals. People taking these drugs are therefore at greater risk of a folic acid deficiency. He notes that malabsorption conditions such as gluten intolerance, celiac disease, leaky gut syndrome, and IBS can also drive the deficiency.

According to Wallach, a vitamin B12 deficiency can arise directly from an inadequate diet. It can also occur secondarily, driven by hypochlorhydria (a lack of stomach acid), by salt deficiency, and by gluten intolerance. In humans, failing to absorb B12/cobalt causes a deficiency disease. It can follow surgical removal of part of the stomach (which wipes out the zones that make intrinsic factor) or of the ileum, small-intestinal pouches (diverticulae), parasites (tapeworm), celiac disease (gluten/grain and cow's-milk-albumen allergy), and other malabsorption disorders. The classic results are pernicious anemia and demyelination — stripping of the myelin insulation — of the spinal cord and the large nerve trunks.

Dermatitis (atopic dermatitis, eczema, and dermatitis herpetiformis) is a common skin disease that Wallach says is treated incorrectly with cortisone or prednisone creams; 97% of these patients have wheat-gluten food allergies and almost as many are sensitive to cow's milk, with the same lesions occurring in the small-intestine lining and causing serious, life-threatening, immune-depleting malabsorption (a precursor to diabetes, cancer, arthritis, and birth defects). Yes -- Wallach reframes many named 'diseases' as malabsorption in disguise. He argues that celiac-type damage to the intestinal lining (from wheat gluten, cow's-milk albumen or soy protein) can destroy up to 85-90 percent of the absorptive surface, so the body starves for minerals even on an adequate diet. On that basis he calls celiac disease the basic cause of many diseases, including diabetes (malabsorption of chromium and vanadium), cancer (malabsorption of zinc, vitamin A and selenium), and muscular dystrophy / cystic fibrosis (malabsorption of selenium). He describes asthma the same way -- a disease of malabsorption with deficiencies of essential fatty acids, manganese and magnesium -- and atopic dermatitis as a malabsorption syndrome.

Wallach uses the pulse test to pin down the individual food triggering irritable bowel syndrome -- commonly wheat, milk, or soy -- then has you eliminate the offending foods.

Wallach says hemorrhoids can be soothed with topical washes or compresses of herbs such as German chamomile, witch hazel, yarrow, horse chestnut, juniper berries, plantain, silver weed and smart weed, or with commercial products like Preparation H.

Wallach describes hydrotherapy as a healing art that began in Roman times and is widely used today by all forms of healing arts, including 'orthodox' medicine. Medicinal baths take many forms — from sitz baths for hemorrhoids and whirlpool for muscle injuries to mineral baths for arthritis — and insurance companies will often pay for some form of hydrotherapy if it is prescribed by a licensed physician of any healing art.

As part of his cancer-prevention program, Wallach lays out a simple ongoing detox routine: take alfalfa daily 'in some form as a detoxifier,' do a liver flush once or twice a month by drinking apple juice for three days, and get a hair analysis each year — which he uses both to monitor toxic-metal load and to check how well you're absorbing minerals (if absorption is poor, he notes, all your mineral levels run low). It sits inside a broader daily regimen for keeping toxins down: dietary fiber at every meal, filtered (not distilled) water, 2 to 3 bowel movements a day, biodegradable household cleaners, and organic food wherever possible. The hair analysis is the feedback loop — it is how he would tell whether the metals are actually coming down.

Dumping syndrome — why an acid intestine disables your enzymes. Dumping syndrome is the sudden emptying of stomach contents into the small intestine all at once, overloading the intestine's natural buffer system. That matters because of where the body's acid is meant to sit: the stomach is supposed to be strongly acidic, the small intestine is not, and pancreatic enzymes require an alkaline environment to function — so when unbuffered acid floods in, they stop working properly. Wallach notes it is a common side effect of stomach surgery, and that anemia and osteoporosis are its common secondary diseases, which is what you would expect from a stretch of gut that can no longer digest and absorb. His treatment works with the mechanism rather than against it: any of the classic bitters such as gentian, folic acid at 3 to 5 mg a day, pectin at half an ounce in water before meals, high animal-protein diets, six to eight small meals a day rather than a few large ones, and lying down for half an hour after eating.

Korsakoff's syndrome is a recent-memory loss that Wallach calls a 'false Alzheimer's disease,' characterized by an inability to record and store new memories — the patient can still perform tasks learned before onset but cannot learn the simplest new ones. It can result from a blow to the head or from chronic alcoholism together with vitamin B1 deficiency, associated with an excess intake of simple carbohydrate and sugar. Confabulation — producing imaginary experiences to fill in what cannot be recalled — is a consistent feature.

Wallach states that when people supplement with plant-derived colloidal copper, their original hair color can come back, spider veins, varicose veins, and hemorrhoids can go away, and some aneurysms can even heal. He presents graying and these vein problems as reversible consequences of a copper deficiency rather than permanent effects of aging.

question: Can a blood test show my eczema is allergy-related?
answer_short: Wallach points to basophils on a standard blood count -- they climb with chronic intestinal allergies, eczema, and asthma (the normal range is about 0-2%), so a high level supports the idea that a food allergy is behind your skin.
claim_text: Wallach notes that basophils on a blood count rise with chronic intestinal allergies, eczema, and asthma, so an elevated basophil level can point to the allergy behind the skin.
verbatim: Basophils (Baso) respond to chronic intesti- nal allergies, eczema, asthma and sometimes with parasitic infestations. The normal range is 0-2%.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Who should take digestive aids, and why. Wallach gives this instruction as part of preventing candidiasis — the Candida albicans overgrowth he ties to chronic fatigue syndrome — and the reasoning is what makes the advice land. Candida is a normally harmless yeast living on the skin, mouth, vagina and intestine. It turns pathological when the gut's competing normal bacteria are killed off by long-term antibiotic use, or when low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, usually the result of salt restriction) lets it move up into the stomach — a location it does not normally occupy. Stress reduces stomach acid once it reaches the point of decompensation, and food allergies change the lining of the gut in a way very similar to celiac disease, raising the nutrient concentration in the gut into a 'hyperfertilized' environment the yeast finds attractive; eventually the overgrowth spills into the bloodstream. So his prevention starts with knowing your own digestive and absorptive patterns: pulse-test for food allergies, avoid long-term antibiotics, and as you grow older take betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal decrease in stomach-acid production. He is emphatic on two more points — take these digestive aids if you are under stress, and deal aggressively with any disease that lowers your immune capacity.

Wallach says long-term antibiotic use kills the normal gut bacteria that hold Candida albicans in check, letting the yeast proliferate, move into the stomach and eventually spill into the bloodstream -- a systemic candidiasis he identifies with chronic fatigue syndrome.
Wallach says eczema is usually caused by food allergies, most often to cow's milk, wheat, and soy, and that pulse tests and elimination diets pinpoint the culprit foods.
Wallach's eczema program includes folic acid at 3-5 mg per day.
Wallach includes zinc at 50 mg three times a day in his internal supplement program for eczema.

Crohn's disease (regional enteritis) is a chronic infiltration of defensive white blood cells and macrophages into the terminal ileum; Wallach attributes it largely to food allergy (such as milk) rather than to the orthodox cortisone-and-surgery approach, noting that rigorous allergen avoidance can prevent acute attacks and reverse the changes to normal. His treatment is a high-fiber diet (pulse-test first to avoid a fiber you are allergic to), folic acid at 5-10 mg three times daily, vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, vitamin B-12 at 1,000 mcg per day (best by injection in this disease), vitamin C to bowel tolerance, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000 mg per day, selenium at 300 mcg three times daily, chromium at 75 mcg three times daily, and zinc at 50 mg three times daily, plus the base-line supplement program and autoimmune urine therapy.

Dermatitis (atopic dermatitis, eczema, and dermatitis herpetiformis) is a common skin disease that Wallach says is treated incorrectly with cortisone or prednisone creams; 97% of these patients have wheat-gluten food allergies and almost as many are sensitive to cow's milk, with the same lesions occurring in the small-intestine lining and causing serious, life-threatening, immune-depleting malabsorption (a precursor to diabetes, cancer, arthritis, and birth defects). His treatment for all three forms is a gluten-free and cow's-milk-free diet, a pulse test on frequently eaten foods, essential fatty acids at 5 gm four times daily, para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) at 200 mg four times daily, betaine HCl and digestive enzymes at 75-200 mg each three times daily before meals, vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, zinc at 50 mg three times daily, and colloidal minerals on top of the base-line supplement program; healing the intestinal lesions takes 60-90 days.

Diabetes, Wallach says, is easy to prevent, cure, and treat (avoiding blindness, hypertension, amputations, early death) — and since 1958 supplemental chromium has been known to prevent and treat both diabetes and hypoglycemia, with vanadium able to replace insulin for adult-onset diabetics. Diagnosis is easy: a six-hour glucose tolerance test shows blood glucose rising steeply (over 275 mg/dL at 30-60 minutes, possibly over 350 and staying elevated) with positive urine sugar. His treatment is chromium and vanadium at 25 mcg per day initially to prevent insulin shock, titrating up to 25 mcg twice then three times daily, then 50 mcg twice daily as insulin is reduced; betaine HCl and digestive enzymes at 75-200 mg three times daily before meals for the celiac-type intestinal lesions from food allergies (wheat gluten, cow's milk, soya); zinc at 50 mg three times daily; B-complex at 50 mg three times daily (including niacin, part of the glucose tolerance factor); essential fatty acids at 5 gm three times daily; vitamin B-12 at 1,000 mcg per day; bioflavonoids including quercetin at 150 mg per day; copper at 2-3 mg per day; lecithin at 2,500 mg three times daily; and glutathione at 100 mg per day, on a high-fiber diet with no processed carbohydrates. Useful herbs include licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra), jaborandi (Pilocarpus jaborandi), yarrow (Achillea millefolium), horseweed (Erigeron canadensis), and Jerusalem artichoke.

question: What is uric acid?
answer_short: Uric acid is a marker of protein metabolism in the liver that spikes during gout attacks; Wallach gives a normal range of 4-8 mg% in men and 4.5-5.5 mg% in women.
claim_text: Wallach describes uric acid as a barometer of protein metabolism in the liver and the blood substance that climbs during gout attacks, with a normal range of 4-8 mg % in males and 4.5-5.5 mg % in females.
verbatim: Uric Acid is a barometer of protein metabo- lism in the liver. It is also the blood substance that accumulates to high levels in attacks of gout. The normal range is 4-8 mg % in males and 4.5-5.5 mg % in females.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: In Wallach's blood-chemistry guide, BUN -- blood urea nitrogen -- gauges how well the liver and kidneys process the by-products of protein metabolism, with a normal range of 10-25 mg%. Moderate elevations point to adrenal and liver disease. A high BUN is a 'red flag' for kidney, thyroid and anterior pituitary disease, while very low BUN is typical of posterior pituitary disease.

Wallach describes menarche/menstruation: the regular monthly cycle alternating ovulation (mid-cycle, about day 14) with the 3-7 day 'period' (discharge of blood and uterine lining). He notes periods often stop in athletes and women who drop below 20% body fat — of no health consequence in itself, but a signal of being too thin for normal cycling and ovulation. Painful periods (which he usually attributes to essential-fatty-acid deficiency) can be severe enough to force bed rest. His treatment for painful or excessive ('heavy flow') menses: over-the-counter products (for example Midol) and/or herbs — snapdragon (Linaria vulgaris), bethroot (Trillium erectum), black cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa), blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides), tamarac (Larix americana), ragwort (Senecio fuchsii), lady's mantle (Alchemilla vulgaris), St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum), shepherd's purse (Capsella bursa-pastoris), white deadnettle (Lamium album) and yarrow (Achillea millefolium); plus essential fatty acids (salmon oil and flaxseed oil) at 5 grams three times a day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 international units per day, selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day, and iron at 25-50 milligrams per day (especially for vegetarian women who don't eat red meat or liver regularly).

Wallach describes potassium as a key 'macro' mineral involved in proper heart rhythm, acid-base balance, osmotic (fluid-pressure) balance and kidney function, and gives its normal blood range as 3.5 to 4.4 mEq/L. He notes that elevated potassium is typical of heart block, adrenal-gland deficiency and hypoventilation. Decreased potassium, by contrast, is typical of diarrhea, hyperactive adrenals, weakness, fatigue, poor posture, palpitations, irregular heartbeat and chronic kidney disease.

Typical copper levels in the blood. Wallach gives average plasma copper as 87–153 mg/dl (women) and 89–137 mg/dl (men). About 90% of the copper in plasma travels bound to a carrier protein called ceruloplasmin.

Elevated cholesterol (above 200 mg per 100 ml of blood) is a risk marker for cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and liver disease, with causes including low-fiber diets, excess vitamin D, essential-fatty-acid deficiency, refined sugar and flour, and poor exercise (Wallach cautions that LOW cholesterol can be as dangerous as high). Treatment is regular exercise, the base-line supplement program, one to two heaping tablespoons of oat bran or protein fiber in juice or vitamin C to bowel tolerance, essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times daily, niacin (vitamin B-3) at 450 mg twice daily as time-release tablets, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, chromium at 75 micrograms three times daily, selenium at 100 micrograms three times daily, evening primrose (Oenothera biennis), and a liver flush.

How acidic your stomach is supposed to be. Wallach draws a sharp line between the body's internal chemistry and its secretions. Internally, acidity is policed within a very narrow range: healthy blood runs 7.36 to 7.44, below 7.30 is acidosis, above 7.44 is alkalosis, and anything below 6.8 or above 7.8 is rapidly fatal. Secretions and excretions are the opposite — deliberately variable, running from about 1.0 in stomach acid at one end to 8.2 in pancreatic juice at the other, with alkaline urine in vegans. That spread is the point rather than a flaw. The stomach is meant to be strongly acidic: it is the acid environment that keeps the stomach sterile and that activates protein digestion. The pancreatic juice meeting food further down the tract is meant to be alkaline — which is why acid conditions in the small intestine disable pancreatic enzymes.

Wallach describes meningocele (severe anencephaly or spina bifida) as a birth defect caused by a deficiency of folic acid, B12, or zinc and vitamin A during early pregnancy, often the result of deficient diets or malabsorption in the mother. He points to a large cluster of anencephaly babies born to migrant workers in McAllen, Texas in the early 1990s: public health authorities attributed it to a chemical pollutant, but Wallach argues it actually appears to be a folic acid and zinc deficiency from the winter diet of poor migrant workers living on corn tortillas. He urges all women of childbearing age to take the 90 essential nutrients before, during, and after pregnancy.

Dr. Wallach ties testosterone directly to the trace mineral boron. He says the body requires boron to maintain normal blood levels of both estrogen and testosterone, and that boron supplementation actually doubles testosterone levels. He describes the effect as fast and measurable: within 8 days, supplementing boron cut urinary mineral losses (40% less calcium, 33% less magnesium, and less phosphorus) and doubled a key estrogen (estradiol) to the levels seen in women on estrogen-replacement therapy — with testosterone likewise doubling. So in Wallach's framework, low testosterone is in part a boron-deficiency problem, and boron is a direct nutritional lever to raise it.

question: Can an underactive thyroid cause cold hands and feet?
answer_short: Wallach links chronically cold hands and feet to low thyroid; his home test is a morning basal temperature below 97.8 taken in the armpit, plus feeling slow in the morning.
claim_text: Wallach says a morning basal body temperature below 97.8, chronically cold hands and feet, and being slow in the morning most likely mean poor thyroid function.
verbatim: your basal body temperature first thing in the morning by placing a thermometer in your axilla (armpit) before stirring out of bed (be sure to shake down the thermometer the night before and place it on the night stand to prevent unnecessary movement); ifyour basal body temperature is less than 97.8 or less, if you have chronically cold hands and feet, and if you are slow in the morning, you most likely have poor thyroid function.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach says an under-active thyroid frequently causes fatigue (and weight gain and edema) even without a goiter, and you can screen for it with a basal body temperature test -- take your temperature under your armpit before getting up, and a reading below 97.6 F indicates low thyroid.

Hypothyroid (low thyroid) states often do not produce a goiter (thyroid enlargement) but instead cause obesity, fatigue, disinterest, low blood pressure, and water retention (edema); diagnose with a basal body temperature test — an underarm temperature below 98°F on waking indicates low thyroid. Treatment: thyroid at 3-9 grains each morning (excess causes rapid heart rate and arm tremor — increase to the overdose level, then back off one grain); kelp; an iodine supplement at 250-500 micrograms per day; and the herb quercus marine (Fucus vesiculosis).

Poor circulation can be caused by cardiovascular disease, low thyroid function, and vitamin E deficiency; its symptoms include cold hands and feet and numb, tingling fingers and toes. Treatment includes EDTA chelation, intravenous hydrogen peroxide, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, massage, hydrotherapy, acupuncture, and herbs including ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba), hawthorn (Crataegus oxyacantha), horsetail (Equisetum arvense), lavender (Lavandula angustifolia), lily-of-the-valley (Convallaria majalis), rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis), scotch pine (Pinus sylvestris), and cayenne pepper (Capsicum minimum).

For poor circulation - which Wallach attributes to cardiovascular disease (arteriosclerosis, low thyroid, magnesium deficiency, and vitamin E deficiency) and which shows up as cold hands and feet and numb, tingling fingers and toes - he includes ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba) among the recommended herbs, alongside hawthorn, horsetail, lavender, lily-of-the-valley, rosemary, scotch pine, and cayenne pepper. These accompany EDTA chelation, intravenous hydrogen peroxide, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, vitamin E, massage, hydrotherapy, and acupuncture.

Iodine is an essential mineral concentrated in the thyroid gland; combined with the amino acid tyrosine it is manufactured into the thyroid hormone thyroxin, which regulates digestion, heart rate, body temperature, sweat-gland activity, the nervous and reproductive systems, general metabolism and body weight. Wallach argues iodine intake is usually low to begin with, and that as Americans restrict their salt intake on medical advice, physician-caused goiter and hypothyroidism have become epidemic; copper is a required cofactor for using iodine, so copper-poor soils also drive goiter. Low iodine and thyroid function produce hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's disease) -- fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hair loss, depression, constipation, dry skin, poor memory, goiter, infertility, and congenital birth defects (cretinism in the newborn). He notes many foods act as goitrogens that interfere with thyroid function (dietary and waterborne nitrates, cruciferous vegetables, gluten intolerance) and that about 11 million Americans have an under- or over-active thyroid; the average American takes in only 170 to 250 micrograms of iodine per day, and metallic iodine is not toxic up to 2,000 micrograms per day.

Menkes' Kinky Hair Syndrome is the genetic disorder Wallach ties most directly to copper. He says it is thought to be a sex-linked recessive genetic defect of copper absorption. Affected infants show stunted growth, defective keratin in the hair (the 'kinky' hair), loss of hair pigment, low body temperature (low thyroid function, anemia), degeneration and fractures of the aortic elastin (aneurysms), arthritis in the growth plates of the long bones, and progressive mental deterioration — the last because the brain is left totally devoid of cytochrome oxidase, an essential copper-dependent enzyme. Because of the copper absorption problem, Wallach says injections of copper and liver extracts plus a diet program designed for celiac patients will be useful for these children.

Dieting (weight loss) succeeds on basic habits, per Wallach: avoid caffeine (it drops blood sugar 30-90 minutes later and creates hunger pangs); drink eight glasses of water daily (thirst is often mistaken for hunger); diagnose contributing problems — food allergies (pulse test), hypoglycemia (six-hour glucose tolerance test), or hypothyroidism (basal body temperature); don't skip meals (eat breakfast like a queen, lunch like a princess, dinner like a pauper) and keep a meal schedule; exercise in moderation on a schedule; take before-meal fiber such as oat-bran diet tabs with water 30 minutes before meals to curb appetite; don't forget the base-line supplements and plant-derived colloidal minerals; take essential fatty acids as flaxseed oil at 5 gm three times daily to normalize fat metabolism; and use thyroid (start with 3 grains, cutting back or adding as needed) if basal body temperature is low (below 98.7°F).
Wallach says the thyroid gland requires all 90 essential nutrients to function properly and make thyroxin, not iodine alone.

Wallach says daily antioxidant-rich food and drink quench the free radicals that raise cataract risk, and puts the optimal intake at 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points a day.

Flavonoids (bioflavonoids), once called vitamin P for their role in small-blood-vessel permeability, are antioxidant, anti-inflammatory plant compounds that support vascular and capillary function and lower cardiovascular-disease risk. Wallach lists the health problems of bioflavonoid deficiency: capillary hemorrhage, reduced immune capacity, widespread free-radical injury and inflammation, hemorrhoids, venous insufficiency, leg ulcers, bruising, nosebleeds, increased cancer risk, shortened lifespan, and reduced telomere length and viability.

Losing weight itself creates the damage antioxidants defend against. Wallach says the byproducts of burning fat can turn into free radicals that inflame the intima, the lining of the arteries, which then drives arteriosclerosis, cardiovascular disease, cancer and Alzheimer's disease. His instruction is not a single daily pill but flooding yourself with multiple antioxidants at every meal, framed as an insurance policy against the free radicals you will eat without knowing it.

Free radicals are molecules carrying an extra unpaired electron, and Wallach quotes Dr. Roy Walford calling them the great white sharks in the biochemical sea. The damage runs in steps: they attack polyunsaturated fats and cholesterol in cell membranes, producing lipid peroxides, which decompose into aldehydes that cross-link proteins, lipids and DNA. The result is membranes that stiffen, so nutrients and oxygen cannot get in and wastes cannot get out. They reach us through skin, breath, food and drink, and are also produced internally during normal metabolism.

Selenium's job is to keep the fats in your cells from oxidizing; vegetable oils are polyunsaturated fats that oxidize easily — especially once heated or hydrogenated into trans fats. So Wallach's warning is about the combination: flood the body with rancidity-prone oils while selenium (the antioxidant that would protect them) runs low, and the oils go rancid inside your cells, driving free-radical damage. He calls high vegetable-oil intake concurrent with selenium deficiency “the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer,” and ties the same pairing — including too much fish oil — to birth defects, arteriosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, and sudden cardiac death. The practical point: to him these oils aren't just empty calories, they actively consume the protection selenium is meant to provide.

Among nuts, Wallach singles out English walnuts as nutritionally special: they are a good source of iron, phosphorus, zinc, potassium, and vitamin E, and — uniquely — the only nut with significant levels of omega-3 fatty acids, the anti-inflammatory fats usually associated with fish. An ounce (about 14 halves) carries 190 calories and 18 grams of fat. He raises them within a broader point that nuts, far from being junk food, are tied to lower rates of heart disease.

Wallach identifies heterocyclic amines as free radicals that form in well-done meat and burnt animal fat. He calls them extremely dangerous, warning that they can raise a person's risk of breast, prostate, and colon cancer by as much as 462 percent. It is the reason he tells people never to eat meat cooked well done or with the fat burnt.

question: What causes leg cramps together with numbness in the legs?
answer_short: Wallach ties severe leg cramps to calcium deficiency and the accompanying leg numbness to a B-vitamin deficiency.
claim_text: In the Maybrick case Wallach reads leg cramps so severe "they were like iron bars" as a calcium deficiency, and the accompanying leg numbness as a B-vitamin deficiency — a vivid picture of mineral-starved legs.
verbatim: Maybrick became seriously ill in April 26, 1889 and his doctor was summoned because of headaches (hypoglycemia or diabetes resulting from chromium and va- nadium deficiencies), numbness ( B,, defi- ciency) of his legs and leg cramps (calcium deficiency) so bad “they were like iron bars.”

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Vitamin D is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium and phosphorus in the bones and teeth, and works hand-in-hand with parathyroid hormone. Wallach calls the modern universal vitamin D deficiency a 'physician-caused disease' -- a perfect storm created by medical advice to avoid the sun, wear sunblock and covering clothing, avoid dietary cholesterol (egg yolks, chicken skin, dairy, saturated fats), and skip vitamin-mineral supplements. He lists the health problems of vitamin D deficiency: facial tics and Tourette's syndrome, twitches and muscle cramps, tetany (full-body cramp) and convulsions, childhood rickets (rachitic rosary, bowed legs, knock-knees, pigeon chest), profuse sweating, restless leg syndrome, enlarged wrists, osteopenia/osteoporosis, periodontal disease, arthritis/osteoarthritis/degenerative 'bone-to-bone' arthritis, bone spurs, kidney stones, uterine fibroids, and a higher risk of cancer.

Muscle cramps (charley horse) are a 'mini' convulsion in the muscle caused by deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, potassium, selenium and/or vitamin E. They range from a subtle eyelid twitch or muscle flutter (fasciculations) in the arms or legs to hard cramps of the feet, calves, back and neck. Prevention is the baseline nutritional supplement program; do a pulse test for food allergies that can cause celiac-type changes and malabsorption, and a hair analysis to check mineral status. Treatment can include liquid colloidal calcium, magnesium and potassium, plus betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day before meals.

Yes. Wallach says selenium was universally thought to be toxic until 1957, when it was found to be an essential trace nutrient. Selenium deficiency causes a whole family of diseases — infertility, miscarriages, cystic fibrosis of the pancreas, animal Sudden Infant Death Syndrome, liver cirrhosis, stiff lamb disease, white muscle disease, muscular dystrophy, anemias, encephalomalacia (which he equates with Alzheimer's disease), cardiomyopathy, and mulberry heart disease. In each case, selenium supplementation prevented the disease and in many cases reversed or cured it — the livestock industry does this for a few pennies a day.

Wallach ties poor appetite to mineral status, not just psychology: deficiencies of the minerals zinc and lithium are associated with anorexia (loss of appetite). In the same discussion he goes further, arguing that anorexia nervosa — usually treated as a psychiatric disease — is often a manifestation of a severe food allergy, since sufferers commonly feel better when they don't eat. His answer is to correct the deficiency, hunt down the offending food (frequently cow's milk, wheat, eggs, or corn), and support digestion with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes alongside the baseline vitamin-mineral program.

For muscle cramps and twitching legs, Wallach's treatment includes liquid plant-derived colloidal calcium, magnesium, and potassium, plus betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 mg three times a day before meals, and he says his Pig Arthritis Formula works like a charm.

Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body, with about 99% in the bones and teeth (as hydroxyapatite) and the rest used as a cofactor for blood clotting, muscle contraction, and the heart's electrical conduction. Wallach states that, contrary to the medical belief that high calcium causes kidney stones, a high dietary calcium intake actually reduces the risk of nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcemia, and kidney stones, and that no fewer than 147 deficiency diseases are attributed to calcium deficiency or imbalance. His Common Calcium-Deficiency Diseases include: osteoporosis (with kyphosis, scoliosis, Dowager's hump, lordosis, spontaneous fractures), receding gums, osteomalacia, myelosclerosis, arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, bone spurs, kidney stones, nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, hypertension, insomnia, calcium deposits (vascular, restless leg, atrial fibrillation), cramps and twitches (Tourette's syndrome), premenstrual syndrome, low-back pain (sciatica), neuropathy (Bell's palsy, trigeminal neuralgia), tetany with convulsions, and panic attacks. In his words: 'There are no less than 147 different deficiency-diseases that are directly attributed to a calcium deficiency or imbalance.'

Magnesium is essential to all living organisms, second only to potassium as an intracellular cation; the adult body holds 20 to 28 grams, about 60% of it in bone. It powers energy production and protein synthesis, muscle contractility and nerve excitability, is a cofactor for countless enzymes, and is a constituent of chlorophyll. Calcium and magnesium play antagonistic roles in muscle -- calcium the stimulator, magnesium the relaxer -- so an excess of calcium can induce magnesium-deficiency signs, and an excess of magnesium inhibits bone calcification. Wallach lists a wide range of magnesium-deficiency diseases and symptoms: asthma, anorexia, menstrual migraines, growth failure, electrocardiogram (ECG) changes, neuromuscular problems, tetany and convulsions, depression, muscular weakness, muscle tics, tremors, vertigo, and calcification of the small arteries and soft tissue. Absorption ranges from about 24% for metallic sources to 85% for plant-derived colloidal sources; fat, phytates and calcium reduce it while vitamin D has no effect. He notes there is no evidence of toxicity up to 6,000 milligrams per day when the kidneys are healthy.

Wallach's rule of thumb for how much a single missing mineral can cost you: on average about ten different deficiency diseases can arise from the absence of any one essential mineral - and calcium is his extreme case, capable of producing as many as 147 different diseases when the body is short of it.

question: Does resveratrol affect amyloid-beta or Alzheimer's plaques?
answer_short: A 2005 study Wallach cites found resveratrol significantly lowers secreted and intracellular amyloid-beta (Abeta) peptides, the peptides tied to Alzheimer's.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach identifies aluminum's known biological function as activating the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase and increasing newborn survival, and reports that Professor Gerhard Schrauzer (former chair of chemistry at the University of California, San Diego) argues it should be classed as an essential mineral for all vertebrates including humans. He stresses that aluminum is remarkably nontoxic at dietary levels -- far less toxic than heavy metals -- and that it competes with calcium absorption, so excess can reduce skeletal mineralization. He explicitly rejects the popular fear that aluminum causes Alzheimer's disease, citing the 1992 Oxford study (Frank Watt and colleagues, in Nature) that found identical brain-aluminum levels in Alzheimer's patients and controls, and the Alzheimer's Society's 2013 position that no causal link has been demonstrated.

Wallach's fourth dementia: Alzheimer's disease, which he calls a 'physician-caused' disease -- produced by lowering the patient's dietary cholesterol and saturated fat, prescribing statin drugs, and directing patients to avoid vitamin and mineral supplements. So his prevention starts with knowing your own digestive and absorptive patterns: pulse-test for food allergies, avoid long-term antibiotics, and as you grow older take betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal decrease in stomach-acid production. He is emphatic on two more points — take these digestive aids if you are under stress, and deal aggressively with any disease that lowers your immune capacity.

Vitamin K is one of the fat-soluble vitamins in Wallach's essential-nutrient framework. Isolated in 1939, it is required by the liver to produce prothrombin and at least five other proteins (clotting factors VII, IX and X and proteins C and S), so the blood can clot normally. According to Wallach, the craving for salt dates back to the very beginning of animals and man and is one of the most basic drives of all living organisms. Carnivores, man or beast, do not show a strong salt craving because meat naturally contains fairly large amounts of sodium chloride. Herbivores and human vegetarians, by contrast, demand large amounts of salt because there is little or no natural NaCl in grains, vegetables and fruit.

Wallach rejects the popular belief that salt is inherently dangerous. He argues that salt itself is not intrinsically harmful; the real problem is that eating salt lets the body falsely perceive it is getting sufficient minerals, so a salt-satisfied craving can mask an underlying mineral deficiency. He calls this the mineral equivalent of the 'empty calorie diet' — just as white flour and sugar satisfy hunger while supplying no protein, essential fatty acids, or vitamins, salt intake convinces the body it has adequate minerals when it may not.

Wallach describes an ancient Chinese belief that gold itself was immortal and that consuming it could make a person immortal as well. A practical obstacle, he explains, was that gold powder could not be absorbed and passed through the intestinal tract unchanged, so alchemists searched for ways to make it usable. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive disease of the central nervous system marked by scattered zones of demyelination (loss of the fatty insulating layer on nerves). Wallach argues that infertility in Americans is primarily a nutritional problem. His table of degenerative diseases accordingly lists deafness under tin (Sn), and he ties the documented generational decline in men's hearing to this deficiency.

question: Is there a traditional herbal remedy for PMS?
answer_short: Wallach recounts a famous historical remedy: Lydia Pinkham's herbal 'Vegetable Compound for Women's Complaints,' based on a Native American recipe and marketed for PMS, dysmenorrhea, amenorrhea, menopausal symptoms and infertility.
claim_text: Wallach recounts that Lydia Pinkham's herbal Vegetable Compound was marketed for PMS, dysmenorrhea, amenorrhea, menopausal symptoms and infertility.
verbatim: Others were old family recipes that worked, such as that produced by Lydia Pinkums alled “Lydia Pinkums’ Vegetable and Herbal Extract for Women's Complaints,” which was marketed in newspapers for PMS, dysmenorrhea, amenorthea, menopausal symptoms, and infertility.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach recounts that Lydia Pinkham's herbal compound — built on an ancient Native American recipe — was marketed for PMS, dysmenorrhea, menopausal symptoms and infertility, and worked so well it made her an American icon.

Iodine is an essential mineral concentrated in the thyroid gland; combined with the amino acid tyrosine it is manufactured into the thyroid hormone thyroxin, which regulates digestion, heart rate, body temperature, sweat-gland activity, the nervous and reproductive systems, general metabolism and body weight. Wallach argues iodine intake is usually low to begin with, and that as Americans restrict their salt intake on medical advice, physician-caused goiter and hypothyroidism have become epidemic; copper is a required cofactor for using iodine, so copper-poor soils also drive goiter. Low iodine and thyroid function produce hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's disease) -- fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hair loss, depression, constipation, dry skin, poor memory, goiter, infertility, and congenital birth defects (cretinism in the newborn). He notes many foods act as goitrogens that interfere with thyroid function (dietary and waterborne nitrates, cruciferous vegetables, gluten intolerance) and that about 11 million Americans have an under- or over-active thyroid; the average American takes in only 170 to 250 micrograms of iodine per day, and metallic iodine is not toxic up to 2,000 micrograms per day.

Wallach recounts that Dr. Samuel Hahnemann, a physician from Leipzig, Germany, 'proved' that Cinchona bark (a malaria cure of the day) gave malaria symptoms to healthy people, and went on to 'prove' hundreds of medications and substances. Hahnemann found that very often the more dilute the preparation, the more dramatic the clinical effect — a long-controversial observation that Wallach notes a 1988 article in Nature magazine supported. Homeopathic dilutions are expressed as 'potencies' on decimal/centesimal scales (e.g. 1X/2X, 1C/2C, with European 1D/2D designations); at a 12C dilution there may be one molecule of the original substance or none (Avogadro's Law), yet Wallach says the 'remedy' still has a homeopathic medical effect.

For amenorrhea (absence or stopping of menstrual periods -- often from low body fat in athletes, dieters, and anorexics, where a 10-15 pound weight gain can restart the cycle), Wallach recommends zinc 50 mg three times daily to bring on the period, essential fatty acids as flaxseed oil 1 tablespoon three times daily, and herbal stimulants: saffron (Crocus sativus) as a tea, black cohosh or squawroot (Cimicifuga racemosa) as a fluid extract, and marigold (Calendula officinalis).

Dysmenorrhea (menstrual pain) is common in Western women — so common it is often considered part of PMS — and can be debilitating; the basic problem is abnormal prostaglandin metabolism, which commercial products mask without addressing. Wallach's treatment is vitamins B-3 and B-6 at 50-100 mg three times daily, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000 mg per day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, and essential fatty acids at 5 gm three times daily, plus the base-line supplements and avoiding caffeine; blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides) and black cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa) are the ideal natural herbs for the pain.

Muscular dystrophy (MD) is, in Wallach's view, a preventable selenium-deficiency disease — he points out it has been eliminated in livestock ('white muscle disease') by giving selenium to pregnant females and fast-growing young animals. Adequate selenium in preconception women maintains pregnancy and prevents all forms of MD (Duchenne, Erb, Leyden-Moebius, Landouzy-Dejerine, Becker's and Gowers), and he adds Keshan disease (a selenium-deficiency heart-muscle dystrophy) to the list. Food-allergy-driven celiac-type changes in the small intestine are a common cause of the tissue selenium deficiency, so do a pulse test. He says giving selenium and vitamin E by intramuscular or intravenous injection at the very first symptoms can arrest or cure the disease. Treatment of MD and/or Keshan disease: selenium orally (as plant-derived colloidal minerals), intravenously or intramuscularly at 50-1,000 micrograms a day (by weight); vitamin E intramuscularly at 80 milligrams a day; selenium orally at 250-1,000 micrograms a day; vitamin E 800-1,200 (orally); sulfur amino acids (a complete amino-acid infusion intravenously, plus free amino acids orally) and sugarless Jello; essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times a day; avoid food allergens; keep fat under 20 percent of daily calories; choline as soy lecithin at 10-20 grams a day; and avoid exercise for the first month of treatment to protect compromised muscle.

Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) has a long history in 'orthodox' medicine — the word derives from 'hysteria,' and the historical treatment was hysterectomy (removing the ovaries and uterus 'cured' the cyclical emotional symptoms but caused an abrupt menopause). It is now known that a deficiency of essential fatty acids, working together with the woman's cyclical hormone patterns, produces the classic PMS picture of fragile emotions, irrational behavior, mania, depression, and debilitating pelvic cramps. Treatment includes vitamin B-6 at 100 milligrams, essential fatty acids three times a day, vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene during the last 14 days of the cycle, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, calcium (especially from plant-derived colloidal sources), and herbs including mistletoe (Viscum album), black cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa), and blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides).

Wallach asserts there are no fewer than 147 deficiency diseases that can be attributed to calcium deficiency or imbalance, and that the entire American diet is critically deficient in calcium. Common calcium-deficiency conditions he lists include osteoporosis, receding gums, osteomalacia, arthritis, hypertension, insomnia, kidney stones, bone and heel spurs, calcium deposits, muscle cramps and twitches, premenstrual syndrome, low-back pain, Bell's palsy, panic attacks, and tetany.

question: Is dark chocolate good for weight loss and energy?
answer_short: Chocolate's cocoagin, theobromine, flavanol and flavonoids are thermogenic and antioxidant, making bitter chocolate an energy generator, weight-loss aid and free-radical neutralizer.
claim_text: Wallach says chocolate is a rich source of cocoagin, caffeine, theobromine, flavanol and flavonoids - compounds that have both thermogenic (energy-generating) and antioxidant properties - making bitter chocolate, in his framing, a great energy generator, a great weight-loss product and a powerful free-radical-neutralizing herb.
verbatim: Chocolate is a rich source of cocoagin, caffeine, theobromine, flavanol and flavonoids. These compounds thermogenic (energy generating) properties and antioxidant properties that make bitter chocolate a great energy generator, a great weight loss product and a super free radical neutralizing herb.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Wallach says daily antioxidant-rich food and drink quench the free radicals that raise cataract risk, and puts the optimal intake at 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points a day.

Flavonoids (bioflavonoids), once called vitamin P for their role in small-blood-vessel permeability, are antioxidant, anti-inflammatory plant compounds that support vascular and capillary function and lower cardiovascular-disease risk. Wallach lists the health problems of bioflavonoid deficiency: capillary hemorrhage, reduced immune capacity, widespread free-radical injury and inflammation, hemorrhoids, venous insufficiency, leg ulcers, bruising, nosebleeds, increased cancer risk, shortened lifespan, and reduced telomere length and viability.

Wallach says the catechins in green tea are the antioxidants credited with significant anti-cancer activity - reducing cancer risk by as much as 90% - and are 100 times more potent than vitamin C and 25 times more potent than vitamin E at neutralizing free radicals. Green tea itself contains xanthines, caffeine, tannins, polyphenols, catechins, flavonoids, oils and fats, and vitamin C.

Wallach explains that kelp and algae take up the ocean's dissolved inorganic minerals - which he estimates at 200,000,000 tons per cubic mile of sea - and convert them into usable organic form, making kelp eaten as a vegetable a significant source of dietary plant minerals.

As part of a weight-loss plan, Wallach advises using a good weight-loss support product before each meal that contains pyruvate (fuel for the Krebs cycle), chromium picolinate, and chitosan, a saturated-fat binder. He describes chromium picolinate's role as allowing carbohydrate and fats to be burned. It is paired with pyruvate for energy metabolism and chitosan to bind fat.

Wallach draws a line between test-tube results and whole-person results, and puts raising ORAC antioxidant activity on the whole-person side. In in-vivo studies he lists flavonoid supplementation as clinically effective for reducing or eliminating allergies, calming vascular and pulmonary inflammation, raising ORAC antioxidant activity, antimicrobial action against bacteria, viruses, yeast and fungus, improving gastrointestinal function, and supporting the immune system in cancer patients. Flavonoids themselves are plant pigments - the yellow, red and blue in flower petals.

Wallach warns that low-carb weight loss is not automatically safe. To lose weight safely and avoid its common pitfalls — heart attacks, liver damage, high blood pressure, Beriberi, arthritis, osteoporosis, periodontal disease, cancer, sudden death, stroke and kidney stones — a dieter must protect against mineral nutritional deficiencies, which he says drive 'psychotic eating,' and against the free-radical damage generated by burning body fat.

question: Can contaminated grain make your skin tingle and crawl?
answer_short: Wallach recounts ergot poisoning from moldy rye -- the likely cause of the Salem 'bewitchments' -- producing paresthesia (itching and prickling), formication (a feeling of ants crawling under the skin), and even dry gangrene of the fingers and toes.
claim_text: Wallach recounts that ergot poisoning from moldy rye produces paresthesia (itching and prickling), formication (a feeling of ants crawling under the skin), and even dry gangrene of the fingers and toes.
verbatim: ‘Symptoms included painful seizures and spasms, diarrhea, paresthesia (itching and prickling), formication (a feeling that ants are crawling under the skin), vomiting, mania, psychosis, hallucinations, headaches, vertigo, and tinnitus. Dry gangrene is the result of vasoconstriction induced by the ergotamine-ergocristine alkaloids produced by the fungus.

tidbit_pool.claim_text: Zinc deficiency, in Wallach's account, produces a wide range of diseases — from congenital birth defects present at birth to degenerative diseases across every age group. He ties an exhaustive list of congenital birth defects to zinc shortage during pregnancy: Down's syndrome; cleft lip and cleft palate; brain defects (dorsal herniation, hydroencephalocele); micro- or anophthalmia (small or absent eyes); agnathia (small or absent lower jaw); spina bifida; clubbed limbs; syndactyly (webbed toes and fingers); polydactyly (extra limbs and digits); atresia (failure to develop limbs, digits, organs, or the anal opening); diaphragmatic, hiatal, umbilical, and inguinal hernias; heart defects; lung defects; and urogenital defects (horseshoe or small kidney, and intersex malformations of the genitalia).

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) works with folate to synthesize DNA and RNA, supports bone marrow and the production of myelin (the nerve-fiber insulation), and is required to release folate from its bound form -- so a B12 deficiency causes a folic-acid deficiency even when folate intake is optimal. Wallach notes the deficiency can be dietary or secondary to hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid), salt deficiency, or gluten intolerance, and lists its health problems: pernicious anemia (macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia), dementia, neuropsychiatric behavior, demyelination of the brain, spinal cord, optic nerve, and peripheral nerves, neuropathy, a sore tongue, general weakness, and liver disease.
Wallach warns that vitamin B6 can cause harm at excessive intakes. The sign of overdose is peripheral neuropathy — nerve damage that shows up in the fingers and legs.

Silver has a long clinical track record that Wallach relays from the older medical literature (presented for reference, not as his own protocol). Colloidal silver was reported in the British Medical Journal (Sir Malcolm Morris, 1917) as soothing rather than irritating - subduing inflammation and promoting healing - and used for enlarged prostate with bladder irritation, pruritus (itching) of the anus, perineal eczema, and hemorrhoids; J. Mark Hovell (1917) reported benefit for the Eustachian tubes, nasal-and-throat congestion (catarrh), and mouth, throat and ear infections; and T.H. Anderson Wells (Lancet, 1918) used it intravenously for a post-childbirth blood infection. Silver sulfadiazine (Silvadene) is used in about 70% of U.S. burn centers and stops the herpes simplex virus behind cold sores.

In Wallach's framework a biotin deficiency in humans produces a progressive loss of both hair and hair color. Alongside the hair changes he describes skin lesions over the nose and mouth, depression, hyperesthesia and paresthesia (especially in the extremities), muscle pain, conjunctivitis, and blepharitis.
Wallach notes the tuberculosis drug isoniazid works against vitamin B6, producing the classic B6-deficiency picture -- including peripheral neuritis (nerve inflammation).

Wallach details the ultraviolet (UV) therapy spectrum: visible light is only about five percent of the total output of UV therapy lamps; the UV ray spectrum ranges between 500 and 3,100 Angstrom units, and 2,537 Angstrom units is the peak intensity — the level that produces the germicidal, erythemic (skin-reddening), and vitamin-D-producing effects.

Wallach argues that an exclusive meat diet fails to supply adequate calcium, even when it includes organ meats such as liver and kidney (which do boost selenium, sulfur, cobalt, molybdenum and zinc). Because it still falls short on calcium, magnesium and manganese, he says the diet produces the "disease pictures" typical of pure carnivores: short stature, arthritis, osteoporosis, tooth loss, "Repetitive Motion Syndrome," aneurysms and skin wrinkles. This is part of his broader conclusion that no single dietary camp — vegan or carnivore — delivers all the minerals the body needs, which led him to a universal concept of supplementing the full set of essential nutrients.
